Title: Driving in the wrong direction? Modelling policy mixes for EV adoption
Authors: Miquel Bassart i Loré, Daniel Torren-Peraire
Abstract: Car-centric societies face challenges in transitioning to sustainable mobility, with electric vehicle adoption depending on the interaction of consumer behaviour, firm innovation, and policy incentives. To examine these dynamics, we develop an agent-based model calibrated on California data from 2001-2023. Heterogeneous consumers influence each other in their acceptance of EVs, while manufacturers incorporate these changes into their innovation and product-mix strategies. We evaluate individual and combined policy instruments, including carbon pricing, new and used purchase rebates, production subsidies, and electricity price subsidies. Results show that only carbon pricing and new vehicle purchase rebates achieve 95% electric vehicle adoption by 2035. Each policy has trade-offs: carbon pricing reduces consumer welfare, while new purchase rebates create heavy fiscal burdens. Policy combinations reduce the intensity of interventions and transitional costs, while mitigating trade-offs. By 2050, combinations of carbon price and subsidies yield 30% reductions in cumulative emissions against the business-as-usual scenario.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Dynamic collaborative optimization of wind-assisted ship energy efficiency under variable navigational conditions
Authors: Diankang Zhang, Kai Wang, Zhongwei Li, Hongzhi Liang, Xinyue Zhang, Ranqi Ma, Lianzhong Huang, Jianyi Wu, Xiaowu Li, Jianlin Cao

Title: Multi-source data fusion for ship carbon emission prediction with language-model decision support
Authors: Xingyun Yan, Jie Hu, Lingyu Wang, Jin Qi, Bin Chen, Mingzhu Fang, Meixing Guo, Hairui Wang

Title: Road contexts shape spatial patterns of bat assemblages in tropical dry forests
Authors: Danny Zurc, Juan Carlos Jaramillo-Fayad, Jordi Viñas, Antonio Guillén-Servent, Jorge Antonio Mejía, Mauricio Corredor
Abstract: Road infrastructure can shape biodiversity patterns, yet evidence from tropical systems remains limited. We assessed variation in bat assemblages across four road contexts (Old, Operational, Under Construction, Mitigation area) and three distances from the road edge (0, 300, 2000 m) in a Colombian tropical dry forest. Assemblages were sampled using mist nets and passive acoustic monitoring and integrated as operational taxonomic units (OTUs). Taxonomic diversity and composition varied among road contexts and sampled distances. After standardization to a common sample coverage, Hill diversity was higher at the sampled 2000 m distance than at 0 m in the Under Construction and Operational contexts, whereas the Mitigation area and Old context showed different spatial patterns. Beta-diversity analyses showed that compositional differentiation among sampled distances involved both taxonomic-unit turnover and nestedness, with the relative contribution of these components varying among road contexts. Guild representation also varied among contexts and distances, with aerial insectivores predominating in most context × distance combinations. Because environmental drivers were not directly measured and each context corresponds to a single site, these results are descriptive rather than tests of causal road effects. These findings reveal context-dependent spatial variation in bat assemblages across the sampled distances and provide a descriptive baseline for designing future studies that explicitly evaluate the mechanisms and spatial extent of road-associated effects.

Authors: Cheol-Heon Jeong, Yee Ka Wong, Nicole Trieu, Christi Jose, Xing Wang, Junshi Xu, Milad Saeedi, Yushan Su, Chris Charron, Arthur Chan, Marianne Hatzopoulou, Greg Evans

Title: Calibrating fiscal policy signals for ammonia fuel adoption in shipping
Authors: Xin Mao, Jiadong Shi, Kum Fai Yuen
Abstract: Ammonia is a promising zero-carbon shipping fuel, yet uptake remains sluggish. This study calibrates budget-constrained fiscal instruments to promote shipowner adoption and sustain diffusion while ensuring supplier profitability, supply stability, and government payoff. We develop a two-layer Stackelberg model with the government as leader and shipowners and fuel suppliers as followers. In the static layer, the optimum is identified by gridding tax and subsidy; in the dynamic layer, ODEs track 100-month trajectories. Results show an interior optimum within the fiscal corridor at 99 , 79 , delivering 99.996 % static adoption, an equilibrium price of USD 1 , 080 / t , and about 87.06 % penetration. Dynamics converge stably, with learning-driven price declines and rising composite government utility. The optimum serves as a policy anchor: maintain the carbon tax as a long-run signal and front-load then phase down the subsidy as adoption increases. Within the corridor, fiscal parameters are adaptively adjusted to observed adoption, profitability, and net fiscal burden.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Heterogeneous bus ridership responses to micro-scale built environment: Evidence from explainable AI
Authors: Andy Angxi Xie
Abstract: Despite the inherent complexity of urban mobility, conventional methodologies often oversimplify the associations between transit demand and built environment, leaving nonlinearity and behavioral asymmetries obscured. This study integrates computer vision and explainable artificial intelligence (XGBoost-SHAP) to decode how the micro-scale built environment affects multidimensional bus ridership. Six environmental visual proxies were extracted through semantic segmentation from 3,736 street view imagery, and subsequently analyzed alongside 8.6 million ridership records over one month across 934 bus stops in Shenzhen, China. Four models distinguish temporal-behavioral patterns (weekday peak vs. weekend off-peak, boarding vs. alighting). The results reveal behavioral heterogeneity: stronger correlations were observed in boarding than alighting demand, while weekend discretionary trips exhibit greater sensitivity to micro-environmental quality than weekday mandatory trips. By quantifying nonlinear threshold effects and diminishing marginal utilities, this study develops a spatial screening matrix that supports planners in flagging environmental mismatches and advancing transit-demand-oriented, data-driven transportation planning.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Modeling Taxi-Metro Competition: Uncovering Nonlinear Influences of Trip and Built Environment Factors
Authors: Xiang Liu, Guocong Zhai, Hongtai Yang, Donggen Wang, Mark Zuidgeest, Hongliang Ding, Xiaobo Liu
Abstract: Understanding taxi-metro competition is crucial for optimizing the modal split where both modes serve overlapping origin-destination (OD) pairs. This study examines the nonlinear factors associated with taxi-metro competition strength in Chengdu, defined as the proportion of taxi trips among the combined taxi and metro trips for each OD pair. To account for bounded competition strength, we propose a hybrid model combining Beta regression with Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (Beta-BART), which achieves better predictive performance than gradient-boosted decision trees and BART. The results show that OD distance has the highest relative importance (6.2%) and that competition strength declines sharply as OD distance increases to about 7.5 km, with little change beyond this distance. Furthermore, land use mix exhibits an inverted-U association, with competition strength peaking near 0.80. Practically, these nonlinear patterns can inform more targeted transport planning. Methodologically, the framework provides a template for modeling proportional transportation outcomes with bounded distributions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: To what extent do green roads generate ecological gains?
Authors: Bojun Zhang, Lin Huang, Jiangwen Fan, Yuhao Wu, Haiyan Zhang, Yuxin Qiao, Xiaochuang Bu, Xinran Miao, Yagang Tong
Abstract: Road expansion in fragile plateau regions can cause multidimensional ecological disturbance, yet the relative performance of green-road sections remains uncertain. We assessed the Tongsai Expressway on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau using a matched-reference structure–quality–function framework integrating propensity score matching, land-cover- and distance-stratified gain analysis, and exploratory interpretable machine learning. Green-road sections showed selective rather than universal gains. Statistically supported gains were concentrated in Green Road 2, particularly woodland quality indicators (NDVI, NDBSI, WET) at 300–500 m and grassland water conservation (12.470–18.618 mm) at 100–500 m, whereas structural and composite-index gains lacked consistent support. Variation in estimated road eco-effects was associated with road distance, land cover, elevation, climate, and built-up proximity. Climate-enhanced matching and equal-primary-dimension weighting retained the main patterns. Because this is a single-corridor, non-replicated case study with section-specific spatial and temporal contexts, the findings represent case-specific associations rather than causal effects of individual green-road measures.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Route-informed planning for medium- and heavy-duty truck charging infrastructure in California
Authors: Runhua (Ivan) Xiao, Miguel Jaller, Anmol Pahwa, Claudio B. da Cunha
Abstract: California freight electrification depends as much on charging access and corridor planning as on vehicle adoption. Public agencies and fleets need evidence on whether depot and public charging networks can support truckload operations without increasing empty repositioning, modeled charging-stop requirements, and route infeasibility. This study develops an operations-based freight charging assessment for mixed diesel and battery-electric truck operations and applies it to controlled California truckload scenarios. Rather than optimizing final station sites, the framework evaluates predefined depot-adjacent and public fast-charging sites through route feasibility, total and deadhead VMT, modeled charging stop rows, active charging locations, and cost-accounting indicators. The results are scenario-level route-record comparisons and do not reflect observed daily truck operations or session-level charging dwell measurements.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Data-driven modelling of passenger-car stock electrification: validation and cross-country scenarios
Authors: Dominik Fink, Harald Lerch, Vladislav Kemka, Pavel Žlábek, Jan Kovanda
Abstract: Electrification policy targets new registrations, but the transition of the national passenger-car stock depends jointly on BEV adoption and vehicle retirement. This study models both, using the Czech Republic as an ageing-market case. A power-law registration function is calibrated on Czech data for 2016–2024 and benchmarked against five reference countries; a fixed-lifetime stock-turnover model, with an age-structured extension, then gives post-2035 trajectories. The adoption parameter α is a reduced-form capacity measure reflecting affordability, policy continuity and charging access. Adjusted MAPE is 6.1–17.2 % with R 2 above 0.92; the Czech in-sample fit gives MAPE 5.8 %, R 2 0.974, α cal 0.034 and n cal 2.81. Vehicle lifetime alone sets the nominal replacement horizon r d = r 0 + L: 2047 for L = 12 years, 2055 for L = 20, while α scn = 0.10–0.40 governs the stock trajectory, not the terminal year. Results are scenario comparisons, not forecasts.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: The collaborative road clearing problem for Post-Disaster emergency response
Authors: Luana Souza Almeida, Alireza Ghasemi, Floris Goerlandt
Abstract: After a disaster, the immediate response operations focus on reducing human suffering by restoring access to essential relief services, while long-term recovery emphasizes infrastructure reconstruction. This study addresses road clearing decisions in the immediate response phase, when restoring critical connectivity is crucial and conventional repair models may be inadequate. Approaches based solely on cost or speed may fail to reconnect the most critical routes for isolated communities. To address this gap, we propose the Collaborative Road Clearing Problem for Post-Disaster Emergency Response, which prioritizes reconnecting affected areas to critical infrastructure such as ports and airports. The model explicitly accounts for collaboration among multiple clearing teams, allowing joint operations on severely obstructed roads. A mixed-integer linear programming formulation and a heuristic are introduced. The numerical experiments demonstrate the benefits of collaboration, particularly in large networks and scenarios with long clearance times.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Sustainable cold recycled pavements: performance, leaching behavior, and life cycle assessment
Authors: Ruisheng Feng, Xu Wang, Shuqin Zheng
Abstract: Sustainable transportation demands resilient infrastructure. While cold in-place recycling (CIR) lowers emissions, moisture susceptibility compromises long-term durability. Existing research rarely integrates micro-scale thermodynamics of alternative fillers with macro-scale lifecycle environmental assessments. To bridge this gap, this study evaluates the thermodynamic, mechanical, and environmental performance of CIR mixtures incorporating steel slag (SS) and rice husk ash (RHA) using surface free energy (SFE), dynamic modulus, contaminant leaching, and life cycle assessment (LCA). Results indicate optimal substitutions (75% SS and 50% RHA) provide favorable multi-scale improvements. For SS-75, SFE increased by 49%, yielding a suitable moisture resistance with a Tensile Strength Ratio (TSR) of 88.97%, while dynamic modulus improved. This structural enhancement permits thinner virgin asphalt overlays, ensuring safe contaminant encapsulation. Consequently, SS-75 reduced global warming potential by 15.2%, energy demand by 16.6%, acidification by 16.2%, and ozone depletion by 12.8%. These findings offer generalizable evidence for environmentally optimized pavement management.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Urban transportation, environment, and community health for New York City (UTECH-NYC)
Authors: Danni Lu, Alireza Yazdiani, Cafer Avci, Carl Closs, Mohammad Tayarani, H. Oliver Gao
Abstract: Urban traffic remains a major source of fine particulate pollution and the related health burdens. We developed an urban transportation, environment, and community health model for NYC (UTECH-NYC), an integrated framework linking travel demand, on-road emissions, dispersion, and human exposure at 20 m × 20 m spatial and hourly temporal resolution. UTECH-NYC enables analysis of transportation policies such as congestion pricing and vehicle electrification. Results show that the NYC congestion toll reduces traffic-attributable PM 2.5 by 16% and exposure by 13% in Manhattan’s central business district, while displacing pollution to peripheral corridors. Furthermore, vehicle-electrification scenarios reduce traffic-attributable PM 2.5 across NYC. However, under the stylized uniform-adoption scenarios considered here, spatially uneven burdens are not fully eliminated, and the distributional implications are sensitive to the equity metric used. UTECH-NYC therefore provides a fine-scale, equity-aware framework for evaluation of urban transportation policies.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Explaining COVID-19 Tokyo metro station-level ridership disruption and recovery: pre-pandemic demand, built environment and centrality
Authors: Xi Lin, Giuseppe Vizzari, Claudio Feliciani, Daichi Yanagisawa, Katsuhiro Nishinari
Abstract: COVID-19 caused severe and uneven metro ridership declines. This study examines station-level annual ridership change in Tokyo from 2020 to 2023 relative to 2019, integrating pre-pandemic demand, built environment, and network centrality. Its main contribution is to identify how these factors shaped ridership resilience from acute disruption to recovery using ordinary least squares (OLS) and geographically weighted regression (GWR). Results show that high pre-pandemic demand and Production and Service intensity are associated with larger proportional losses, especially in 2020–2021. Road density is consistently linked to smaller declines and stronger recovery, indicating the importance of local access networks. Land-use mix becomes increasingly positive during recovery, suggesting that functionally diverse station areas better supported localized daily activities. Destination accessibility and centrality show more spatially uneven and temporally unstable effects. These findings suggest that resilience-oriented planning should combine targeted operations for vulnerable high-demand stations with local access improvements and mixed-use station-area development.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Deployment-oriented validation of vessel energy efficiency inference for maritime decarbonisation policy
Authors: Xun Yang, Ran Yan
Abstract: AI-based vessel fuel-consumption models are used for emission accounting, compliance screening, and decarbonisation planning, but their reported accuracy depends on how validation is designed. Using high-frequency data from 27 ocean-going vessels, this study tests whether random mixed validation overstates model performance. We compare it with maritime use-case tests for later-period prediction, unseen trips, unseen vessels, cross-type transfer, and data-scarce transfer. Across 64 model-task combinations, use-case-aligned held-out errors are 9.18 percentage points higher on average than random mixed-validation estimates. Prediction error also reverses direction across settings, indicating that accuracy metrics alone can hide policy-relevant over- or under-estimation. In a container-ship CII case study, rating accuracy ranges from 34.4% to 71.7%, while 11.7% to 100.0% of action-required D/E vessel-years are missed. These results indicate that regulatory and planning applications require validation aligned with the intended maritime use case, with reporting of both error magnitude and bias direction.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Do aviation hazard rankings overlook conservation-concern birds in U.S. wildlife strikes?
Authors: Amir Rafe, Subasish Das
Abstract: Airports concentrate aircraft and birds in shared space, making wildlife strikes a flight-safety problem and a documented source of avian mortality. We analyze 343,997 U.S. wildlife-strike records from 1990 to 2025 with a framework that corrects for reporting growth, models per-strike severity, and ranks species by aviation hazard and conservation status. A detection-aware count model bounds the true rise in the strike rate between 3.4 and 8 fold, below the widely cited fourteen-fold rise in the reported rate. A random-parameters ordered probit shows that engine ingestion and body mass dominate severity, with the mass effect growing more variable at higher impact speeds. Conservation weighting shifts 112 of 310 ranked species by more than 30 places, elevating aerial insectivores, migratory warblers, and grassland passerines, including the Vulnerable Chimney Swift. The results support region- and season-specific mitigation that protects aircraft and declining birds together.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Challenges in comparing measured and modelled annual average noise levels around airports
Authors: Rebekka C. van der Grift, Alireza Amiri Simkooei, Mirjam Snellen
Abstract: Aircraft noise has a significant impact on communities near airports. To regulate noise, annual average levels such as L den are modelled across large areas. This study examines the consistency between L den predicted by the European Civil Aviation Conference Doc 29 model and measurements from noise monitoring terminals around Amsterdam Airport Schiphol from 2017 to 2024. While strong correlations confirm Doc29′s suitability for system-level assessments, systematic biases persist, with nighttime levels L night generally overestimated and L den underestimated. Three potential sources were identified: difference between modelled and flown tracks, background noise influencing measured levels, and undetected flights, particularly for quieter aircraft and in low noise regions. Accounting for these factors improves correlation and reduces deviation between measurements and predictions. These results demonstrate promising methods for enabling noise model validation near airports. Further improvements in detection methods and operational modelling will increase the robustness of noise assessments and better support evidence-based policy development around major airports.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Pragmatism, not ideology: drivers of e-bike sharing usage intensity
Authors: Michael Stiebe, Frank Christian Krysiak, Widar von Arx, Benjamin Weggelaar
Abstract: What drives usage intensity among registered e-bike sharing system (EBSS) users – distinguishing power users from dormant registrants – remains underexplored despite its importance for system viability. We link survey responses from 1,844 registered users to their individual trip histories within an operational dataset of 1.4 million trips from free-floating S-Pedelec and dock-based e-bike sharing systems operating concurrently in Basel, Switzerland. Using Gaussian Mixture Model clustering and an ordered logit model, we find that usage is highly concentrated (Gini = 0.77) and primarily substitutes public transport. Pro-environmental self-identity negatively associates with high-intensity user (“power-user”) status. Instead, intensive use is associated with multimodal integration and perceived functional superiority over public transport. System design distinguishes two distinct pragmatic archetypes: dock-based “routine optimizers” and free-floating “flexibility maximizers”. These findings suggest EBSS policy should emphasize multimodal integration and service reliability calibrated to EBSS’s genuine but bounded role in sustainable urban mobility.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: How does harassment alter cycling satisfaction? Insights from London
Authors: Khashayar Kazemzadeh, Amir Pooyan Afghari, Ahmadreza Faghih Imani, Jonas De Vos
Abstract: Cycling satisfaction is a key factor in increasing cycling mode share, particularly in low-cycling contexts such as England. Satisfaction is subjective and shaped by both observable conditions and unobserved psychological factors. One important but understudied factor is harassment, which can take many forms (e.g., verbal, physical, sexual, racial, or identity-based) and may strongly influence cyclists’ experiences. This study develops a quantitative framework to examine how harassment affects cycling satisfaction through a latent variable representing harassment-related experiences, using survey data from 1,525 cyclists in London. Results show that cyclists who feel stressed, unsafe, or threatened are significantly more likely to report dissatisfaction, even after controlling for socio-demographic factors. Harassment-related perceptions are strongly associated with traffic exposure, lighting conditions, and accumulated near-miss or collision experiences. These findings demonstrate that cycling satisfaction is significantly associated with harassment-related perceptions and highlight the need to incorporate harassment-sensitive measures into cycling level-of-service evaluations.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Contextualising the impact of street slopes on pedestrian accessibility for sustainable mobility
Authors: Vasileios Milias, Panagiotis G. Tzouras, Ioanna Vourdanou, Konstantinos Markos, Konstantinos Kepaptsoglou, Alexandros Nikitas
Abstract: Proximity-based planning has become a central paradigm in transport policy, guiding the design of sustainable, accessible, and liveable cities. This shift has driven the development of various methods for assessing pedestrian accessibility, reflecting the central role of walking as the most sustainable mode. Yet, the impact of street slopes on accessibility is often neglected and remains poorly understood. This study identifies two systematic biases: a slope-speed bias, caused by assuming flat terrain, and a slope-preference bias, reflecting behavioural aversion to slopes. We compare three models: (a) slope-agnostic, (b) slope-adjusted with gradient-dependent speeds, and (c) slope-preference incorporating walking preferences across walking propensity groups. Applied in Athens, Greece, results show that slope-agnostic models overestimate accessibility by approximately 6–8% on average. Accounting for walking preferences introduces an additional 33–40% reduction for low-propensity walkers across destination types. The proposed framework offers a transferable approach for integrating terrain sensitivity into accessibility analysis.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Emission reduction potential of freeway stop-and-go wave smoothing
Authors: Junyi Ji, Derek Gloudemans, Gergely Zachár, William Barbour, Jonathan Sprinkle, Benedetto Piccoli, Daniel B. Work
Abstract: The real-world potential of stop-and-go wave smoothing at scale remains largely unquantified. Smoothing freeway waves requires opening a gap large enough for them to dissipate, but that gap is often impractically large. We propose a counterfactual wave-smoothing benchmark that reconstructs a smooth, feasible trajectory from each empirical trajectory by solving a quadratic program with fixed boundary conditions and a maximum-gap constraint, and we use the MOVES model to estimate the resulting emission reduction potential. Applying the framework to nine weeks of weekday peak-period data from the I-24 MOTION testbed, which exhibits rich day-to-day variation in wave dynamics, we find meaningful potential for passenger cars under a 0.1-mile maximum-gap constraint: average CO 2 reductions of 9.80% to 14.08% across lanes, with 12.94% to 25.70% in CO, 24.29% to 29.76% in HC, and 29.40% to 36.03% in NOx. Trucks emerge as particularly attractive targets, showing roughly twice the reduction potential of passenger cars.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: An integrated simulation and optimization framework for mixed-fleet public transit decarbonization
Authors: Majid Gholami Shirkoohi, Walter Mérida
Abstract: Public transit agencies face growing pressure to decarbonize operations while maintaining reliable service. Planning and operating mixed fleets of diesel, battery-electric, and hydrogen buses requires modelling tools that capture interactions among vehicle energy use, charging and refueling infrastructure, and network operations. This paper presents MLTransit, an integrated simulation-optimization framework that links general transit feed specification preprocessing, agent-based operational modelling, and multi-stage optimization to evaluate transit decarbonization strategies under realistic service patterns. The framework represents vehicle energy consumption, nonlinear charging behavior, queueing at charging facilities, battery degradation, emissions, and grid constraints. A two-stage optimization assigns service blocks to feasible vehicle types and determines cost-efficient charging infrastructure and policy parameters, while detailed charging schedules emerge endogenously through simulation. Applied to the Metro Vancouver bus network, MLTransit evaluates trade-offs between depot-only and combined depot-opportunity charging, showing that combined charging improves operational feasibility and service reliability at the cost of higher infrastructure investment.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Understanding e-cargo bike substitution of car, cycling, and walking through domestic trials in three UK cities
Authors: Labib Azzouz, Noel Cass, Zhaoqi Zhou
Abstract: This study examines ECB mode substitution using a mixed-methods approach combining travel diaries from 42 households participating in real-world ECB trials across Leeds, Oxford, and Brighton with 111 interviews. ECB trips mostly replaced car travel (60%), followed by conventional cycling (23%) and walking (17%). Regression analysis showed that car substitution was more likely among men, older adults, retirees, multi-car households and for passenger-carrying, shopping, child-escorting, and leisure trips. Qualitative findings further described a gradual process of building confidence, adapting routines, and integrating the ECB into everyday mobility, enabling progressively greater car substitution. For some, the ECB was viewed as a realistic alternative to a second car. The findings show that ECBs offer a versatile family mobility solution with substantial sustainability potential by reducing vehicle mileage and emissions, while supporting transitions towards car ownership renunciation. The study details targeted policy interventions that can maximise ECBs uptake and their contribution to sustainability.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Managing autonomous vehicle accessibility to mitigate environmental rebound effects
Authors: Sunghee Lee, Jooyoung Kim
Abstract: Autonomous vehicle (AV) services can improve urban mobility, but excessive door-to-door convenience may shift users from public transport and increase zero-occupant vehicle (ZOV) circulation. This study treats AV access time as a policy-controllable variable and evaluates its environmental and operational effects under fixed peak-hour demand. An integrated framework combines synthetic demand preprocessing, multi-modal user equilibrium assignment, explicit ZOV loading, and reinforcement-learning policy search. Results show that reducing access time below about five minutes sharply increases empty vehicle movements, total system travel time, and CO 2 emissions. Within a restricted generic road-charging framework, a six-minute access time with a moderate per-trip charge forms a constrained Pareto-knee. Extending the policy space to ZOV-targeted instruments, including empty-VKT charges, reduces reliance on generic road charges and improves network performance, reducing CO 2 emissions by up to 15.0% relative to the fixed reference condition (Base=100) while preserving public transport shares.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Integrated AHP–Entropy–Game Theory and GIS framework for EV charging station site selection
Authors: Fahri Alp Erdoğan, Murat Başeğmez, Mehmet Alper Akdemir, Murat Sağbaş, Halim Kazan
Abstract: The rapid growth of electric mobility requires robust frameworks for optimal electric vehicle charging station (EVCS) deployment. This study proposes an integrated spatial decision-support framework combining the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP), Entropy Weight Method (EWM), game-theoretic deviation-minimization weighting, and Geographic Information Systems (GIS) to identify suitable EVCS locations in İzmir, Türkiye. The approach integrates literature-informed AHP-based prioritization with entropy-derived analytical weighting for balanced multi-criteria spatial analysis. Results show that proximity to electricity transmission lines receives the highest weight and should be interpreted as an infrastructure-proximity and potential grid-connection feasibility proxy, rather than a direct measure of grid capacity or electricity-system adequacy. Population density and major accessibility factors, including main roads and transport stations, contribute to suitability as indirect demand and mobility proxies. Highly suitable zones are mainly concentrated in central and northern districts (Konak, Karşıyaka, Bornova, Bayraklı), covering 6.51 % of the area, while 17.08 % is classified as suitable.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Explaining temporal and spatial variability in shared e-scooter ridership in Christchurch, New Zealand
Authors: Wai Chi Goldie Leung, Katarzyna Sila-Nowicka, Lindsey Conrow, Grant McKenzie, Simon Kingham, Vanessa Brum-Bastos
Abstract: Shared electric scooters (e-scooters) are widely adopted, yet their ridership patterns remain insufficiently understood. Existing studies rely on origin–destination (OD) inferred trips and use global models, which overlook true paths and spatial heterogeneity effects. This constrains understanding of spatio-temporal patterns and drivers of shared e-scooter ridership, reducing the effectiveness of transport planning and policy interventions. We address these limitations using observed street-segment-level trip counts to identify spatio-temporal ridership profile by clustering hourly ridership curves. We also apply Geographically Weighted Poisson Regression (GWPR) to examine spatial associations between ridership and contextual factors. Results reveal clear temporal differences from cycling behaviour and strong spatially varying associations between ridership and built environment, which global models fail to capture. Our findings show that data-driven clustering can classify micromobility behaviour without assuming trip purpose. Although focused on Christchurch, the methodological framework is transferable and applicable to other cities with similar data.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Wildfire shrinks shelter access unevenly across California
Authors: Fatemeh Janatabadi, Alireza Ermagun
Abstract: This study advances disaster decision-making by embedding wildfire expected annual loss (EAL) into cumulative shelter access measurements across California. Departing from conventional metrics that assume full facility availability during wildfire events, it applies an EAL-weighted adjustment across multiple travel-time thresholds. Three findings emerge from the multi-scalar analysis at the census block group and county levels. First, EAL weighting consistently reduces shelter access and reveals geographically uneven proportional losses within counties. Second, county-level disparities are most persistent where extensive wildland–urban interface (WUI) development, uneven shelter distribution, concentrated wildfire exposure, and limited transportation networks coincide. Longer travel-time thresholds reduce within-county disparities in many counties yet do not eliminate structural access constraints in WUI-dominated counties. Third, although EAL-weighted access does not reveal systematic racial disparities, inequities persist by income and vehicle ownership. The framework supports mitigation-oriented identification of structurally vulnerable communities before wildfire occurrence and informs risk-aware resource allocation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Unraveling divergence in pavement LCA tools through attribution analysis
Authors: Jin Li, Wei Sheng, Yuhong Wang
Abstract: Specialized life cycle assessment (LCA) tools are increasingly used for pavement sustainability assessment, yet they can yield divergent results for the same project. This study compares five representative tools—MIT Streamlined Pavement LCA & LCCA Tool, LCA Pave, HERMES CO 2 , Athena Pavement LCA, and asPECT—using four harmonized pavement cases for a 1 km × 3.5 m lane over 50-year period. For embodied/infrastructure-related GHG emissions, project-level tools gave comparable estimates; for the asphalt freeway case, MIT, LCA Pave, and Athena ranged from 364 to 435 t CO 2 -eq/lane-km. When operational emissions were included, PVI-related use-stage effects accounted for 71 %-89 % of full life-cycle GHG in MIT and Athena. Attribution analysis shows that divergence mainly arises from system boundary, LCIA method, traffic-fuel baseline, roughness-fuel modelling, albedo treatment, and recycling-credit assumptions. Tool disagreement should therefore be interpreted modularly by life-cycle stage to guide future improvement.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Corrigendum to “Public or private? A unified demand–supply coupled framework for EV infrastructure investment” [Trans. Res. Part D: Trans. Environ. 159 (2026) 105501]
Authors: Shuhua Hong, Tianjia Yang, Yang Song, Xianbiao (XB) Hu
Abstract: The authors regret that a typographical error appeared in Eq. (34) of the above article. The surrounding text correctly states that each candidate site can be selected by at most one entity. However, the mutual exclusivity constraint was displayed with a non-strict inequality sign (“≤”) instead of the intended strict inequality sign (“<”). Eq. (34) was published as (formula presented) The correct form of Eq. (34) should read (formula presented) This error is confined to the displayed mathematical expression in Eq. (34). The intended mutual exclusivity condition was correctly implemented in all analyses and computations. Therefore, the correction does not affect any numerical results, findings, or conclusions of the study. The authors would like to apologise for any inconvenience caused.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Understanding the heterogeneity of willingness to share: Ridesplitting’s adoption and usage frequency
Authors: Yite SUN, Xiaobing LIU, Yufeng ZHANG, Hua ZHONG, Xuedong YAN, Ziyou GAO
Abstract: Ridesplitting, a shared urban mobility service, is widely regarded as a promising way to alleviate the negative impacts of ride-hailing, yet its market penetration remains low. Existing studies provide limited understanding of spatiotemporal and user heterogeneity in willingness to share (WTS). To fill this gap, we conduct a questionnaire survey in Beijing and apply latent class analysis to identify user segments based on psychological factors related to ridesplitting. Binary logit model and scenario analysis are then used to examine sharing behavior and mode conversion across segments. Results show that both ridesplitting and non-ridesplitting users exhibit substantial heterogeneity in WTS. Moderately satisfied users show strong potential for more frequent use, while improving travel time reliability and cost savings can convert likely adopters into active participants. These findings inform policies and platform strategies to promote sustainable urban mobility.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Dual-dimensional vulnerability assessment of urban road network system under unexpected subway failures
Authors: Xiangjie Yang, Mingyuan Zhang, Sirui Li
Abstract: The unexpected subway failures cause numerous passengers to gather, exerting pressure on the urban road network system (URNS) through their complementary relationship. This study proposes a dual-dimensional vulnerability assessment framework for the URNS under the unexpected subway failures, encompassing both internal functionality and external environment. First, the dependence between subway stations and road intersections is established to quantify transferred passenger flows. Second, a load-capacity model is developed, which treats the surge in origin–destination traffic demand as the triggering condition for cascading effect. Finally, by correlating the functional degradation of the URNS with the resulting increase in carbon emissions, dual-dimensional vulnerability assessment metrics are proposed. A case study of Futian District, Shenzhen, indicates that subway line criticality differs across dimensions. The findings provide a decision-making basis for enhancing the resilience of subway–road transport systems while balancing operational functionality and environmental impacts.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: An evaluation method for the fume emission intensity of rubber-modified asphalt binders
Authors: Guoqiang Sun, Qiyi Zhang, Jiangcheng Ai, Guangchen Wang, Weidong Ning, Bin Li, Long Cheng
Abstract: Accurately quantifying fume emission intensity from rubber-modified asphalt binders is essential for sustainable construction and air-pollution mitigation. This study proposes an evaluation method based on maximum emission rate, peak concentration, and total emission amount. Feasibility was verified through variability, sensitivity, and comparative analyses. The method was applied to rubber-modified asphalt binders at different activation temperatures and multi-source aging durations to quantify fume emission intensity. Microscopic mechanisms were analyzed using fluorescence microscopy (FM), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR). Results indicate good reliability, with parallel experimental variability of 4.94% and a deviation within ±0.03 in weighted sensitivity analysis. Microscopic observations corroborated the macroscopic emission trends: high-temperature activation damaged the rubber structure and increased its solubility, more than doubling fume emission intensity, whereas multi-source aging reduced light components and decreased emissions by approximately 20%.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Impact of environmental functions on electric vehicle charging experience considering contextual constraints
Authors: Chenxi Liu, Hongyuan Lu, Lingbo Liu, Peng Tian, Zhenghong Peng, Hao Wu, Zhigang Li
Abstract: As the electric vehicle market expands, improving public charging experience has become critical to the sustainability of urban transport. Using Wuhan as an empirical case, this study develops a double machine learning framework to examine how urban functional environments shape charging experience through charging behavior, while incorporating competition intensity and time-of-use tariff differentiation as contextual constraints. Based on tens of millions of charging records, three main findings emerge. First, the functional environment has a significant positive causal effect on charging experience, about 60% of which is mediated by charging behavior. Second, only a few behavior types generate disproportionate experience gains, and these behaviors are linked to the joint presence of particular nearby urban functions. Third, moderate levels of competition intensity and time-of-use tariff differentiation amplify both the total effect and behavioral mediation. These findings inform station siting, operational optimization, and charging-network planning.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Carbon-efficient ride-pooling at intercity railway hubs: Nonlinear topological mechanisms and algorithmic insights
Authors: Zechao Ma, Tianqi Gu, Jiayan Zhang, Long Cheng, Inhi Kim, Bin Yu
Abstract: Ride-pooling (RP) can reduce transport emissions, but its carbon reduction potential across spatial contexts remains unclear, especially at intercity transfer hubs. Using citywide regulatory ride-hailing data from Suzhou, China, this study examines how meso-level path topology features are associated with carbon reductions in railway station pooling. Railway station pooled trips show 62.6% higher carbon reductions per trip than the overall pooled-trip sample average, influenced by nonlinear mechanisms and interaction patterns rather than higher pooling intensity. An explainable machine learning framework shows that carbon efficiency is primarily associated with route quality, as reflected in path topology, operational scenarios, and built environment factors. In particular, detour constraints, common drop-off configurations, and their interactions with distance act as critical thresholds. Building on these insights, we develop a dual-layer classification framework that can identify pooling matches with high carbon reduction potential prior to dispatch (accuracy ≥ 96%). These findings suggest that intercity railway stations may serve as favorable contexts for low-carbon RP when demand concentration and route quality align. This insight can help guide matching strategies that are enabled by AI and informed by carbon efficient in shared mobility systems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Promoting energy transition in shipping: An evolutionary game analysis of green corridors
Authors: Haiwei Gu, Michael G.H. Bell, Ze Wang, Zhiqi Shao, Veronica Schulz, Glenn Geers
Abstract: Green corridors are emerging as a practical mechanism to promote alternative fuels. This paper develops an evolutionary game model to better understand the interactions between shipping lines and cargo owners within a green corridor. A population of 15,000 TEU container ships traveling between Australia and Singapore is simulated to study the economic feasibility of three alternative fuels: liquefied natural gas (LNG), methanol, and ammonia. The results indicate that LNG and methanol have a competitive advantage, while ammonia appears less economically attractive under the assumptions and parameter settings adopted in this study, primarily because of its higher associated costs. Sensitivity analysis reveals cargo owners’ willingness to pay (WTP) for alternative fuels, port discounts, and carbon tax significantly influence the fuel transition. It confirms the shipping industry is likely to be particularly sensitive to the cargo owners’ preference for alternative fuels. The study also highlights the importance of coordination among key stakeholders.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Drive or breathe? Information-aware mode choice under real-time exposure using ICLV-CMXL approach
Authors: Rashmi Choudhary, Amit Agarwal
Abstract: Commuters in urban areas face prolonged exposure to air pollution. This study assessed whether providing commuters with real-time, trip-specific air pollution information can encourage a shift towards public transit modes. Sequential integrated choice and latent variable model with a correlated mixed logit component is developed using stated choice data and user perceptions for motorized transport users in Delhi. Real-time pollution information for current modes was obtained through a multimodal router. Perceptions included air quality awareness, availability and usability of air quality information, and willingness to change behavior for primary trips. The results indicate that people with a better understanding of air quality information and its usage are inclined to choose public transit. Motorized two-wheeler users are more sensitive to exposure compared to car users, showing a stronger preference for public transit. These findings highlight the importance of real-time information in mode shift. Policymakers can formulate strategies to reduce individuals’ exposure in public transit.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Robust low-carbon ship routing under weather uncertainty: a distributional reinforcement learning approach
Authors: Turgay Battal
Abstract: Maritime transport carries most global trade yet contributes roughly 3% of greenhouse-gas emissions, and as the IMO targets a 20–30% reduction by 2030 and the EU prices maritime carbon, deterministic routing is increasingly inadequate. This study merges distributional reinforcement learning with distributionally robust optimization for low-carbon routing under spatial weather uncertainty. A quantile-regression deep Q-network (QR-DQN) captures stochastic weather impacts, a Wasserstein-metric DRO term addresses train–deployment distribution shift, and a physics-informed reward embeds hydrodynamic resistance and carbon-intensity compliance. On the Rotterdam–New York corridor, the framework cuts fuel use by 17.9% versus slow steaming and 5.1% versus a standard DQN (about 390 tonnes of CO 2 per voyage, with direct EU ETS and CII relevance), while keeping adverse-weather exposure near zero and fuel variability low. Ablations attribute this consistency mainly to the physics-informed reward, with the critic securing stable training and efficiency and the robust layer curbing tail degradation under shift.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Impacts of speed limits on emissions, energy consumption and traffic efficiency
Authors: Shi-Teng Zheng, Junfang Tian, Rui Jiang, Bin Jia, Ying-En Ge
Abstract: A field experiment is conducted to investigate operational benefits of speed-limit control in platooning traffic, where the leading vehicle travels at a constant cruise speed while an additional speed-limit control is imposed on following vehicles. First, the effects of speed limits on traffic oscillation dynamics and traffic flow performance are analyzed. Results indicate that restricting the maximum speed of vehicles can stabilize traffic flow, reduce oscillation frequency, and lower emissions and energy consumption (EEC), but may reduce traffic throughput due to an increase in platoon length. A simulation framework is then developed to extend this investigation to broader speed levels and bottleneck scenarios. The results show that speed-limit control should vary with cruising speed to balance EEC and traffic efficiency, and that the proposed solutions apply to traffic management strategies. These findings enrich our understanding of traffic dynamics under speed-limit control strategies and provide practical insights for their real-world implementation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Development of regional heavy-duty vehicle driving cycles based on optimized Markova chain
Authors: Yitao Shen, Peng Guan, Shuojin Ren, Zheyu Wang, Sen Chen, Xiao Ma, Jianfu Zhao, Shijin Shuai
Abstract: Driving cycles are essential for vehicle energy and emission standards, but standard cycles often overlook regional variations. This study proposes a novel framework for constructing representative driving cycles for heavy-duty vehicles by optimizing a Markov chain with a hybrid Multi-Population Genetic Algorithm and Wavelet Threshold Denoising (hMPGA-WTD). The methodology involves: (1) spectral clustering of 1.27 million telematics data points to identify operational scenarios; (2) generating scenario-specific cycles using a two-dimensional Markov chain; and (3) enhancing driving cycle fidelity with hMPGA-WTD to reduce feature distortions. The method achieves a mean relative error of 4.61% across key parameters, with velocity standard deviation error below 1%. It outperforms micro-trip concatenation and conventional Markov approaches. Fuel consumption is validated via real-world and chassis dynamometer tests under identical loads, showing a 4.26% deviation, better than the 7.71% under CHTC-TT. The framework offers a robust basis for efficiency assessment and standard development.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Slow and steady wins the race: How autonomy facilitates long-haul truck electrification
Authors: Anthony Wiskich
Abstract: This paper examines how autonomy affects the competitiveness and operations of battery-electric long-haul trucks. We model fleet operations between Sydney and Melbourne—Australia’s busiest long-haul corridor—using a parameterised cost-minimisation framework. By lowering travel-time costs, autonomy leads to slower optimal speeds and reduced energy use. This enables smaller, lighter battery packs or reduces the number of charging stops en route, lowering total costs. Autonomy thus enhances the economic case for battery-electric trucks, improving their cost competitiveness relative to diesel trucks commensurate with an AUS$34/kWh reduction in battery pack price (ranging from about AUS$10 to AUS$75/kWh across sensitivities).
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Enhancing sustainability and cost-efficiency in urban rail-road bridge: A Bayesian-optimized surrogate-assisted framework
Authors: Sentayehu Lelisa Dirirsa, Yan Gao, Qing He, Paul Schonfeld, Jianping Hu
Abstract: Cities increasingly require sustainable and land-efficient transportation infrastructure. While Integrated Rail-Road Bridge (IRRB) optimizes urban land use by combining rail and road into a single bridge, integration alone is insufficient to minimize environmental and economic burdens. Consequently, as horizontal alignment is the primary determinant of economic and environmental footprints, optimizing horizontal geometry is imperative for developing land-efficient and sustainable urban corridors. To address this, we propose a Bayesian-optimized surrogate-assisted Multi-Objective Horizontal Curve Optimization (MOHCO) framework. It comprises a data-driven phase for initial impact datasets, a Bayesian-optimized surrogate model for rapid, high-fidelity impact predictions across high-dimensional design spaces, and a Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm (NSGA-II) multi-objective optimization incorporating CO 2 emissions and contribution to local temperature. Applied to a real-world case, the framework achieved high predictive accuracy (R2 > 0.98), reduced cost by 5.64%, environmental impact by 38.90%, and improved safety by 44.40% compared to manual designs, supporting sustainable urban transportation development.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Getting there and feeling better: mechanisms from perceived accessibility to subjective well-being
Authors: Jiahang Liu, Qiyang Liu
Abstract: Accessibility matters for subjective well-being, yet its underlying mechanisms remain insufficiently understood. Using survey data from 5591 respondents in ten Chinese cities, this study examines how perceived accessibility relates to hedonic and eudaimonic well-being through domain-specific travel satisfaction and social exclusion. After accounting for the indirect pathways, the structural equation modeling results show that perceived accessibility remains positively associated with flourishing and negatively associated with negative affect, whereas its total effect on positive affect is not significant. The mediation effect varies across travel domains and well-being outcomes. Leisure travel satisfaction emerged as the most important mediator for flourishing, while shopping travel satisfaction played a mediation role across all outcomes. Commute travel satisfaction was particularly salient for affective well-being. Social exclusion, meanwhile, constituted a strong and consistent pathway. The findings highlight that accessibility contributes to well-being not only through reaching destinations, but also through satisfying travel experiences and social inclusion.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Bus fleet electrification: A comprehensive review of charging, operations, planning and sustainability
Authors: Federico Silvestri, Seyed Mahdi Miraftabzdeh, Michela Longo, Dario Zaninelli
Abstract: Battery Electric Buses (BEBs) are increasingly adopted by Local Public Transit (LPT) companies to support the sustainable mobility transition, at the cost of introducing new challenges and constraints. This paper presents an up-to-date review of more than 100 studies published between 2019 and 2025 on bus fleet electrification. The analysis identifies four major research directions: Charging Infrastructure and Methods, Bus Fleet Operations, Electrification Planning, and Sustainability. Recurring themes emerge, including the central role of optimized charging strategies on total cost of ownership and the need for integrated planning models that jointly consider infrastructure, battery sizing, and operations. The review also reveals persistent gaps related to uncertainty modeling, scalability for large transport networks, and careful consideration of battery degradation. Finally, a functional framework is proposed to synthesize how current research contributions map onto the practical decision layer, providing a consolidated foundation for future studies and supporting practitioners in large-scale BEB deployment.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: A multi-criteria readiness assessment of cities for sustainable autonomous vehicle infrastructure
Authors: Ertugrul Ayyildiz
Abstract: This study develops an integrated decision-support framework for assessing the readiness of major Turkish cities for sustainable autonomous vehicle (AV) infrastructure. İstanbul, Ankara, İzmir, Bursa, and Antalya are evaluated using 16 sub-criteria grouped under Physical Infrastructure, Smart Mobility, Sustainability, and Adaptive Capacity. Expert judgments are consolidated through the Modified Delphi method and analyzed using Pythagorean Fuzzy Indifference Threshold-based Attribute Ratio Analysis (PF-ITARA) and Pythagorean Fuzzy Measurement of Alternatives and Ranking according to Compromise Solution (PF-MARCOS). The results identify Economic Feasibility, Municipal Capacity, and R&D Ecosystem as the most influential criteria. İzmir ranks first, followed by İstanbul, Ankara, Bursa, and Antalya. Sensitivity analyses confirm that İzmir remains the leading city under alternative threshold structures and 32 criterion-weight perturbation scenarios. The findings show that autonomous vehicle readiness depends on balanced technological, financial, institutional, and sustainability capabilities and provide practical guidance for urban infrastructure planning and phased deployment.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: A framework for sustainable robotaxi infrastructure in emerging cities
Authors: Orhan Engin, Ömer Kaya
Abstract: This study proposes an integrated planning framework for robotaxi deployment in medium-sized cities by combining MCDM, GIS-based spatial analysis, and robustness assessment. Intended primarily for local governments and urban transport authorities, the framework also provides operators and investors with an analytical baseline for fleet sizing and charging-infrastructure planning. Seven main criteria and 32 sub-criteria were weighted using FWZIC and RANCOM, with strong agreement confirmed by Pearson correlation (r = 0.9620), Spearman correlation (ρ = 0.9643), and MAD (0.00728). A normalized [0–1] suitability map was used to delineate feasible service areas. The baseline scenario assumes 200 robotaxis, including 150 active and 50 standby vehicles, with rem-based allocation for staging. Using Tesla Model Y Juniper data as a proxy, total grid-side fleet energy demand was estimated at 9.96 MWh/day. Peak-period sizing indicates that at least nine DC fast-charging units are required for the daytime DC charging component.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Investigating and comparing user experiences at EV charging and petroleum fueling stations
Authors: Aaron I. Rabinowitz, Vaishnavi Karanam, Sina Nordhoff, Scott Hardman, Gil Tal
Abstract: Light duty electrification requires DC charging stations to take over the current role of petroleum stations. However, charging and fueling systems differ substantially in technology, user behavior, and business models. This study analyzes thousands of reviews for petroleum stations and DC charging stations. Using a mixed-methods approach combining quantitative rating, sentiment analysis, and Large Language Model (LLM)-assisted topical classification, factors that shape user experience are identified. Charging and fueling are perceived as fundamentally different activities. Fueling reviews are dominated by fuel price and staff interaction, while charging reviews emphasize equipment reliability, location convenience, and access to nearby amenities. Manufacturer-owned charging networks are perceived more positively than open networks. Open networks suffer from small station sizes and higher outage rates which reduce effective capacity and generate negative feedback. Across networks, proximity to amenities strongly influences perceived convenience and satisfaction. These findings identify actionable pathways for improving charging experiences and perceptions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Decarbonizing the maritime sector: cold ironing and e-fuels. Case study: Gran Canaria
Authors: Pablo Yánez-Rosales, Paula Ferreira, Julieta Schallenberg-Rodriguez, Alexis Lozano-Medina, B.del Rio-Gamero
Abstract: This research addresses the decarbonization of the maritime transport considering the services that can be provided at port, by analyzing both cold ironing and e-fuels production. To this end, the electricity demand for both processes is estimated, as well as the resulting electricity generation cost and the associated emissions, enabling an estimate of the climate neutrality cost. Two possible scenarios were considered for the renewable e-fuel production: dedicated renewable farms versus renewable surpluses coming from the island electricity system. For the cold ironing different scenarios are being considered: electricity coming from the grid and renewable farms to produce the required electricity. The island of Gran Canaria (Canary Islands, Spain) is considered as the case study. The results show a potential reduction of 483 kt of CO 2 -eq (9) % of the island’s emissions) and a levelized cost of energy ranging from 181 to 616 €/MWh, depending on the scenario and e-fuel considered.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Equity by design in electric vehicle charging infrastructure networks
Authors: Yen-Chu Wu, Eleftheria Kontou
Abstract: Public charging infrastructure extends electrified miles, reduces range anxiety, and promotes electric vehicle adoption. However, charging stations remain inaccessible to underserved and disadvantaged populations. To address this, we propose a novel location model for equitable electric vehicle charging infrastructure placement, with objectives to minimize detours for charging and improve trip completion for low-income travelers and multi-unit dwelling residents, who face shorter electric vehicle ranges and limited home charging access. A genetic algorithm-based approach with column generation is used to solve the multi-objective nonlinear bilevel programming problem and identify Pareto-optimal solutions. The proposed method is applied to the state of Illinois transportation network as a case study. We assume universal electric vehicle adoption to represent a forward-looking public planning scenario, rather than calibrating infrastructure solely to current ownership patterns that reflect existing socioeconomic disparities. The results show that our equity-by-design siting improves accessibility for disadvantaged travelers while maintaining service quality and performance for all privileged users. Through analysis of various scenarios, we offer insights into the robustness of equitable charging station placement. Our analysis indicates that (i) siting meeting only cost efficiency priorities can coincide with equitable outcomes but represents only a subset of Pareto-optimal solutions, whereas planning charging location driven by equity reveals various alternatives; (ii) the fewer the charging stations, the more missed trips that leave lower-income and multi-unit dwelling residents and travelers the most vulnerable; (iii) in the early stages of transportation electrification, when charging infrastructure is sparser, it is likely that disparities in charging access will be observed among socioeconomic groups but as the charging network grows denser these accessibility gaps will be bridged.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Ports in transition: rethinking hydrogen hub site selection through a multi-stakeholder lens
Authors: Lara Pomaska, Gordon Wilmsmeier, Johannes Meuer
Abstract: Green hydrogen is central to decarbonizing energy and transport systems, with ports increasingly positioned as key locations for hydrogen-related activities. However, the specific functions of ports within emerging hydrogen value chains and the evolving multi-stakeholder dynamics surrounding their development remain underexplored. The objective of this study is to develop a conceptual multi-actor multi-criteria decision-making framework for hydrogen hub site selection in ports. Drawing on a narrative literature review and expert interviews, we identify four distinct functions in the hydrogen value chain: industrial hydrogen hubs, bunkering-oriented hubs, import–export gateways, and distribution and aggregation nodes. Each function involves specific infrastructure requirements, stakeholder constellations, and decision criteria. By incorporating stakeholder salience and function-specific objectives into the decision logic, our framework structures early-stage decision-making around divergent interests and governance complexity. We contribute to the port development and infrastructure planning literature by introducing hydrogen-related port functions, conceptualizing their evolution, and integrating multi-stakeholder governance into decision-making.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Passenger-freight shared mobility for decarbonizing urban-rural bus systems: fleet and capacity optimization
Authors: Jiabin Wu, Zijian Huang, Linhong Wang, Yiming Bie, Yuting Ji, Jun Gong
Abstract: Urban-rural public transport faces a self-reinforcing cycle of declining ridership, service deterioration, and mounting deficits, while parallel diesel freight operations generate substantial carbon emissions along the same corridors. Passenger-freight shared mobility (PFSM) addresses both challenges by using idle bus capacity to co-transport parcels, yet its implementation must balance passenger service quality and freight efficiency. This study formulates a bilevel optimization model that jointly determines fleet composition, and dynamic capacity allocation, and vehicle scheduling while incorporating stochastic travel time effects of freight operations. An improved jellyfish search algorithm is developed to solve the resulting mixed-integer program. A case study of two urban–rural routes in Shanxi Province, China, shows that the optimized PFSM scheme turns a daily operating deficit of RMB 2462.16 into a profit of RMB 537.55, eliminates dedicated freight trucks, and reduces annual freight-related CO 2 emissions by 19.12 tons per route, demonstrating a viable pathway for decarbonizing rural transport.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Real-world battery electric vehicle charging and driving behavior estimation and quantification
Authors: John Merickel, Casey Quinn, Timothy Coburn, Kang-Ching Chu
Abstract: Newer, longer-range electric vehicles (EVs) drive approximately 12,000 miles annually, approaching the 14,000-mile annual average for gas vehicles, highlighting the importance to understand better EV charging and driving behavior as EVs become mainstream. Using U.S. EV driving, parking, and charging data from 2018 to 2019 and 2023–2024, we analyzed how drivers use charging infrastructure and predicted charging likelihood. A random-forest model was used to screen for key factors, informing an interpretable mixed logit model with about 80 % out-of-sample accuracy. Drivers of longer-range EVs in 2023–2024 primarily charged at home, but plugged in roughly 25 % less often at home at the end of the day than drivers of shorter-range EVs when state of charge was 50 %. Charging was more likely (∼5–9 %) in the Northeast than in other regions, particularly in winter. Additionally, greater public charging availability may also be associated with an increase in the probability of away-from-home charging.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Tracking sustainability dynamics in EU transport sector: Bayesian latent change-score analysis study
Authors: Alexandru Constăngioară, Olimpia Ban, Mirela Bucurean, Adriana Mirela Constăngioară
Abstract: This dataset contains harmonized longitudinal data for the EU-27 covering the period 2007–2023, designed to support empirical analysis of transport-sector greenhouse gas emissions dynamics. It includes transport-related greenhouse gas emissions per capita (GHG), road freight activity measured in tonne-kilometres (TK), and Logistics Performance Index (LPI) scores. GHG emissions and freight activity data were sourced from Eurostat, population data from the UN World Population Prospects (via Our World in Data), and LPI scores from the World Bank. The dataset integrates these sources into a consistent country-level panel structure. All variables were log-transformed and standardized prior to analysis to address skewness and scale differences. Time alignment was performed to match the availability of LPI waves, resulting in harmonized observation periods suitable for longitudinal and latent change score modeling. The dataset includes the processed wide-format file (DATA_wide.xlsx) used in the empirical analysis, along with associated metadata required for replication. It is intended for use in studies on transport emissions, logistics performance, sustainability transitions, and dynamic panel or structural equation modeling.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Enhancing transportation system resilience under earthquake-induced geohazards: a framework for cross-regional rescue
Authors: Damin Zhou, Li Peng, Rui Guo, Zhousong Jiang, Muzi Li
Abstract: In mountainous areas, earthquake-induced geohazards frequently fragment road networks, isolating dispersed rural settlements and overwhelming local disaster response. Resource allocation constrained by fixed administrative boundaries often fails to adapt to the connectivity of road networks. We propose a coupled simulation framework that integrates an agent-based model with network science to strengthen the resilience of transportation systems in response to earthquake-induced geohazards. This framework simulates cascading failures in transportation system functionality that affect human mobility, enabling the assessment of how physical disruptions constrain organizational decision-making. Sensitivity and robustness analyses addressing macrolevel environmental constraints, microlevel behavioral attributes, and conditions under cross-factor scenarios revealed that this approach substantially enhances system resilience, particularly under high disaster intensity and limited resources. This study shows that improving transportation system functionality during disasters requires aligning emergency management strategies with the topological realities of networked mobility.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Predicting moose (Alces alces) activity at roadside mineral licks: Implications for moose-vehicle collisions
Authors: Beatrice Penco, Roy V. Rea, Chris J. Johnson, Gayle Hesse, Marco Apollonio
Abstract: Moose-vehicle collisions (MVCs) are a substantial cause of mortality for moose throughout some portions of their range. We investigated a series of factors that explained the timing of moose visits to roadside mineral licks (RMLs) in north-central British Columbia, Canada. Roadside mineral licks are formed by the pooling of road de-icing agents and are attractive to moose, which use them to supplement mineral intake. Moose activity was monitored with camera traps deployed at four RMLs over a 12-year period. Generalized linear mixed models suggested that snowpack and spring green-up best accounted for annual variation in the timing of spring and summer peaks of lick use by moose. Our findings can help to guide road safety planners as they develop site- and season-specific measures for mitigating MVCs which helps to increase public safety and conserve moose.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Socio-technical barriers to electric mobility in India: an expert-based integrated modelling analysis
Authors: Roma Kandpal, Izuru Saizen
Abstract: Electric mobility is central to decarbonising transport; however, developing economies face persistent systemic barriers that limit the transition from fossil fuel-based transport. This study explores India’s case using an expert-based multi-criteria approach to map influences and hierarchical positions among 16 critical socio-technical barriers. These barriers were refined from a set of 29 barriers that were previously identified through a literature review and subsequently prioritised by domain experts. The analysis suggests that, from the perspective of experts, high purchase costs, limited domestic manufacturing capacity, and underdeveloped battery supply chains had the greatest influence on this transition, whereas charging infrastructure constraints and maintenance gaps reinforced these barriers. The cultural attachment to gasoline vehicles is perceived as a deep socio-technical constraint. The findings indicate the importance of leverage points, including cost-reduction strategies, coordinated policies to support domestic manufacturing, and accelerated deployment of charging infrastructure to support electric vehicle transition in India.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Public transport availability, delayed learning to drive and later life car dependence
Authors: Shane Timmons, Adam Joachim Shier, Peter D. Lunn
Abstract: High levels of car dependency are a major challenge for decarbonisation policy. This paper explores how early-life mobility environments shape long-run driving behaviour through two underexplored questions: whether public transport access predicts delayed learning to drive and whether the age at which individuals learn to drive is associated with later driving intensity. We merge nationally representative survey data from Ireland ( N > 2,000) with Public Transport Accessibility Level (PTAL) scores to model (1) age at learning to drive, using survival analysis, and (2) recent driving behaviour, using a hurdle regression model. Higher public transport accessibility is associated with significantly later learning, with individuals in high‑PTAL areas 30% less likely to have learned by age 20 than those with no access. Each year of delayed learning predicts a lower likelihood of weekday driving and a 2% reduction in Vehicle Kilometres Travelled (VKT) on driving days. The findings have implications for understanding the long-term benefits of public transport provision.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: LCA-based comparisons of alternative powertrains of city buses using real-world driving cycle
Authors: Rokom Perme, Gitakrishnan Ramadurai
Abstract: The transportation sector is a major contributor to global emissions, making shifts to mass transit and low-emission powertrains essential. This study conducts a Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) of diesel, Battery Electric Buses (BEBs), and Hydrogen Fuel Cell Electric Buses (HFCEBs) using two approaches: Aggregate Emission-based LCA (AE-LCA), based on average fuel consumption, and Real-world Driving Cycle LCA (RDC-LCA), using GPS-derived driving cycles with second-by-second emissions estimated using CMEM and COPERT 5.6. Across all powertrains and energy pathways, RDC-LCA estimated higher Global Warming Potentials (GWPs) than AE-LCA, with deviations ranging from 8.66% for BEBs charged using captive renewable energy to 36.48% for diesel buses. HFCEBs supplied with green hydrogen achieved up to 85.50% lower GWP than diesel buses, while BEBs exhibited the lowest GWP under decarbonized electricity pathways, including renewable energy and nuclear power. These findings highlight the importance of considering vehicle powertrains and upstream energy sources to minimize transport-sector GWP.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Private vs social costs of vehicle adoption and ownership: a sales-weighted analysis
Authors: Franklin Simmons, Jay Wu
Abstract: The economic competitiveness of battery electric vehicles (BEVs) relative to internal combustion engine vehicles (ICEVs) remains an important question for transportation and climate policy. Existing studies have largely relied on representative vehicles or scenario-based assumptions, providing limited insight into current market outcomes. This research develops a sales-weighted framework using observed sales of best-selling U.S. light-duty vehicles to evaluate both total cost of ownership and total societal cost, which incorporates carbon externalities and government purchase incentives. Results show that BEVs remain more expensive than comparable ICEVs due to higher BEV capital costs outweighing gains from lower operating costs. Monetizing carbon emissions using the societal cost of carbon reduces, but does not eliminate, the societal cost difference under 2024 market conditions. These findings suggest that economically efficient transportation electrification requires continued reduction in BEV purchase costs, electricity-sector decarbonization, and policies that more fully internalize the societal cost of carbon emissions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Total cost of ownership for CO2 carriers under alternative fuel price uncertainty
Authors: Kyunghwa Kim, Wook Kim
Abstract: As environmental regulations become more stringent, the maritime industry faces increasing pressure to make informed decisions on alternative fuels and power systems amid substantial uncertainty in fuel costs and regulatory shifts. This study develops a techno-economic assessment framework for a CO 2 carrier operating under stringent phased European Union (EU)’s environmental regulations. Economic dispatch analysis combined with Monte Carlo simulation evaluates three conventional genset systems and six alternative-fueled fuel cell (FC) systems. This study adopts the mean and the 95% value at risk (VaR 95% ) of the total cost of ownership (TCO) as comparative metrics. The results indicate that the blue liquid hydrogen (b-LH 2 ) FC system achieves the lowest mean TCO and VaR 95% , while the electro-methanol (e-MeOH) FC system has the highest in both metrics. Notably, VaR 95% rankings differ from those based on mean TCO, underscoring the importance of risk-based evaluation. This framework supports risk-aware investment decisions for shipowners facing market volatility.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Direct and indirect impacts of road networks on vegetation cover
Authors: Ziheng Huang, Qingjie Fu, Huixin Lin, Jingyang Liu, Lanyi Zhang, Min Wu, Xisheng Hu
Abstract: Road expansion balances socio-economic growth with ecological threats to vegetation cover, yet quantifying and comparing direct and indirect effects remains a challenge. This study analyzes road-vegetation dynamics (2015–2023) in Fujian, China’s first Ecological Civilization Pilot Zone, using a direct/indirect impact framework coupled with geospatial explainable artificial intelligence (Geo-XAI). Results show rising road density alongside slight vegetation recovery.
