Direct impact exhibits a strong negative linear correlation with road density, governed by nighttime light in cities and population density in rural areas. In contrast, indirect impact is predominantly positive, nonlinear and spatially heterogeneous, primarily governed mainly by land use intensity. Nonlinear thresholds exist nighttime light intensifies direct losses above 35 but promotes indirect gains only above 60.5; population density exacerbates direct impact up to ∼ 5,070 persons/km2, while supporting indirect benefits only below ∼ 1,270 persons/km2. The findings underscore the need for spatially targeted, pathway-specific management to harmonize infrastructure and conservation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Integrated traffic assignment model for evaluating shared mobility impacts on urban transportation
Authors: Mobina Nankali, Grace Arndtsen, Michael W. Levin
Abstract: Shared mobility affects congestion, infrastructure, accessibility, and emissions. This paper integrates a logit choice model with a user equilibrium (UE) model to capture complexities of transportation network companies, bike sharing, and car sharing. We extend a standard UE framework by embedding shared mobility operational constraints, including fleet-size limits and rebalancing trips, enforced through a penalty function that separates the problem into two subproblems solved using the traffic assignment by paired alternative segments algorithm. We provide the first large-scale numerical analysis of integrated shared mobility impacts on the Minneapolis–St. Paul metropolitan network, which has 3061 nodes and over 9.3 million origin–destination pairs. A sensitivity analysis examines the effects of transportation network companies pricing, shared electric vehicle promotion, and micro-mobility removal on congestion, rebalancing intensity, and accessibility. Results show that minor parameter adjustments significantly influence network-wide travel behavior, traffic patterns, and emissions estimated using the motor vehicle emission simulator (MOVES).
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Monitoring-based macroscopic refinement model for urban traffic noise under varying flow conditions
Authors: Yiquan Xu, Hequn Min, Yajing Di, Wei Ling, Quan Ding, Ronghua Huang
Abstract: Urban traffic noise prediction commonly depends on traffic-based emission models, which demand extensive input data yet show limited accuracy under dynamic traffic conditions. This paper develops a noise monitoring-based macroscopic refinement model that estimates equivalent source power levels of urban traffic flow through roadside measurements. The model characterizes traffic flow as a discrete line source under free-flow conditions or a continuous one under congested flow, with source power levels derived from monitored noise and road-geometry data. Validation across four Nanjing arterials demonstrates that the model achieves mean absolute errors of 0.8–2.5 dB(A) and root mean square errors of 1.1–2.9 dB(A), showing lower errors than traffic-based approaches. An empirical reference based on flow speed ratio (Formula presented) for source model selection was derived from systematic performance evaluation across the tested scenarios. The framework demonstrates that roadside noise monitoring provides a practical basis for equivalent source power estimation under varying urban traffic conditions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Agent-based modelling of urban non-exhaust emissions reveals the limits of fleet electrification
Authors: Marc Sturrock
Abstract: Non-exhaust emissions from brake and tyre wear are now the dominant source of traffic-related particulate matter, complicated by heavier electric vehicles. Such particulate also includes road-surface wear and resuspended dust, but Dublin’s frequent rain suppresses them, so we calibrate the two dominant channels: brake wear (ultrafine particles, UFP) and tyre wear (PM 2.5 ). We build a high-resolution, moving-observer agent-based model of the Phibsborough junction, Dublin, calibrated against street-level Google Air View data, to evaluate passenger-preserving policy scenarios. Global sensitivity analysis reveals an interaction-dominated system where traffic dynamics rival fleet composition. Electrification benefits depend entirely on regenerative braking: UFP at 50% spans −19% (with regen) to + 13% (without), while PM 2.5 rises 1 to 5% from added mass. Bus modal shift gives the largest dual-pollutant gains (−30% UFP, −34% PM 2.5 at 50%). A 30 km/h limit cuts UFP 16.5% independently of fleet; a combined policy delivers −27% UFP and −12% PM 2.5 .
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: When closer is not better: travel well-being among peri-urban older adults
Authors: Panyu Peng, Yibin Ao, Yangxi Lv, Mingyang Li, Hao Zhu
Abstract: Transportation-related subjective well-being captures emotions and satisfaction during travel and is increasingly used to evaluate the social benefits of transport and spatial policies. Using survey data from older adults in peri-urban Chengdu, China, we examine the associations of objective accessibility, perceived built-environment quality, perceived accessibility, and mobility capability with travel well-being and overall well-being. This study combines structural equation modeling, explainable machine learning, and robust interaction regressions to examine structural pathways, nonlinear patterns, and conditional associations. Perceived built-environment quality and mobility capability are positively associated with travel well-being, which is, in turn, positively associated with overall well-being. By contrast, higher objective accessibility is associated with lower travel well-being on average. This negative association tends to weaken at higher levels of perceived built-environment quality and mobility capability. The findings suggest that improvements in proximity alone may be insufficient and should be accompanied by safe, comfortable, continuous, predictable, and barrier-free walking conditions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Noise, ferries patterns and residents’ perception: the port of Las Palmas case
Authors: Eduardo Hernández-Pérez, Beatriz Tovar, Salvador del Saz-Salazar
Abstract: Managing acoustic externalities at the port-city interface requires integrating source emissions with community perception. This study develops a framework to characterise ferry noise during hotelling, combining high-resolution monitoring with social analysis. Methodologically, AIS-synchronized measurements characterised vessel emissions, while a stratified survey evaluated resident annoyance. Results reveal L den levels of ∼67.5 dBA, exceeding industrial limits due to tonal and low-frequency penalties. These findings demonstrate that strategic maps and point measurements serve complementary purposes: the former for urban planning and the latter for designing market-based mitigation incentives to supports the ’polluter pays’ principle. Furthermore, despite low self-reported noise disturbance, hierarchical regression analysis identified residents’ health risk perception and pro-environmental behaviour as key predictors of annoyance. Specifically, the model established health risk perception as the primary factor driving heightened sensitivity. Within normalised urban noise context, concern for physical well-being acts as the principal catalyst for perceived annoyance, surpassing both ideological and contextual factors.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Editorial Board
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Assessing the public charging serviceability for electric vehicles: an accessibility-based approach
Authors: Yuzheng Xie, Wenying Ji
Abstract: This study proposes a serviceability assessment framework for public electric vehicle charging infrastructure (EVCI) that evaluates tract-level supply–demand gaps using charging miles per public-charging-dependent electric vehicle (EV) per day. In this framework, user exposure to reachable charging opportunities is estimated using a customized Gaussian two-step floating catchment area accessibility model that incorporates mobility-informed spatial competition. This exposure is then converted into a physically interpretable serviceability metric to provide a planning-level indicator of the estimated balance between accessible public charging service and expected charging demand. A case study in Arlington, Alexandria, and Falls Church, Virginia, USA, shows strong sensitivity to detour tolerance, with the median gap shifting from 4.54 under a 5-minute detour to − 4.45 under a 15-minute detour. Cross-scenario diagnosis indicates three decision-relevant deficit drivers: sparse supply presence in residential and suburban tracts, throughput limitations in mixed-use activity centers, and competition-sensitive coupling effects along major corridors under expanded reachability.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Electric vehicle driving range optimization considering vehicle-to-grid technology in China
Authors: Chikun Huang, Chaoxu Xu, Zhenhong Lin
Abstract: Determining the optimal driving range for battery electric vehicles (BEVs) is crucial to meet user needs while minimizing production mismatch costs. The introduction of vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology complicates this, as bidirectional energy flow reduces battery lifespan. This study develops a framework to determine the optimal range, considering time-of-use pricing, V2G revenues, range limitation, and battery degradation. Results show users prefer longer ranges when V2G benefits are significant. In the base case, a 400 km range meets 93.54% of user needs without considering V2G or degradation. When discharging revenue per kWh exceeds 2 times the peak-to-valley price difference, users are incentivized to choose longer ranges. Charging during shoulder periods and discharging during peak hours increases range by 4.8%; considering battery degradation, the increase is 3.4%; and when both factors are considered, the range increases by 8.8%. Waste in range, materials, and emissions is calculated based on these results.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Social tipping in electric mobility? Lessons from the electric vehicles lead market
Authors: John Thøgersen, Marianne Aasen
Abstract: In most countries of the world, the diffusion of battery electric vehicles (EVs) is still limited to “innovators.” Only in Norway have EVs been so widely adopted that they have reached the “early majority” (i.e., more than 16% of the car stock). To learn what others can do to follow the front-runner, this paper reports a study of drivers and barriers of EV adoption in Norway based on a yearly, representative rolling panel survey from 2018 to 2023, interviewing more than 4000 residents per year. In Norway, the transformation to EVs was initiated by an ambitious demand-side policy. Cross-lagged panel analyses reveal that, in this context, supportive social norms were important drivers of EV adoption, amplified by self-reinforcing feedback loops, as suggested by innovation diffusion theory and research on “social tipping.” Social norms nudging may hence be a tool to accelerate the diffusion of EVs, complementing financial and infrastructure measures.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Commute time thresholds across different city scales in urban China
Authors: Jiaxue Shang, Jianhui Yu, Li Chen, Bin Zhang, Wenzhong Zhang
Abstract: Long commutes are typically considered undesirable, yet in China’s super cities, residents endure significantly longer commutes without necessarily reporting lower satisfaction. To explain this phenomenon and systematically examine the differentiated thresholds of commute satisfaction across city scales, this study adopts reference point theory and analyzes large-scale survey data from 59 Chinese cities using a two-stage machine learning approach. Results indicate that commute time is the most influential factor, with satisfaction thresholds rising alongside city scale—from 19.0 min in small cities to 43.5 min in super cities. City size moderates satisfaction in a U-shaped pattern, with a rebound in super cities linked to better transport infrastructure and social comparison effects. Thresholds also vary across commuting modes. From a behavioral economics perspective, the research clarifies the psychological mechanisms behind commute well-being, providing a scientific basis for tailored urban transport policies that enhance residents’ health and quality of life.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Port decarbonisation readiness of container Terminals: An Interval-Valued fuzzy TOPSIS approach
Authors: Turgay Battal, Yeliz Çelik, Meltem Eken
Abstract: Ports are essential elements of global supply chains, yet their progress towards decarbonisation varies widely. This study develops a Port Decarbonisation Readiness Framework (PDRF) to evaluate the readiness of six container terminals in Türkiye. The framework integrates three components: entropy-based weighting of sustainability indicators, interval-valued fuzzy representation of uncertainty, and a fuzzy Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (fuzzy TOPSIS) ranking procedure. The PDRF assesses terminal-level readiness across Scope 1 and 2 operational emissions and Scope 3 mitigation readiness for onshore power supply (OPS). Because Scope 3 emissions from shipping operations are difficult to quantify, they are represented through mitigation-readiness indicators (OPS planning and electrification potential) rather than a full inventory. The results reveal substantial differences in decarbonisation readiness among terminals and demonstrate how the PDRF can support port authorities and policymakers in identifying priorities and aligning port strategies with climate goals.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Does public debt hinder transport decarbonization? Theoretical analysis and empirical evidence
Authors: Yunhan Zhang, Zhixin Liu, Le Wen, Douglas J. Wilson
Abstract: Transport CO 2 emissions have become one of the fastest-growing sources of global greenhouse gases, posing a major challenge to sustainable development. This study examines whether, and under what conditions, public debt supports or hinders transport-sector decarbonization. We extend the debt-environment model to the transport sector, demonstrating a nonlinear U-shaped long-run relationship between public debt and transport CO 2 emissions, and test it using a panel CS-ARDL approach for 31 economies from 2000 to 2021. The empirical results support a nonlinear U-shaped long-run relationship between public debt and transport CO 2 emissions. Additionally, transport-related climate change mitigation technologies and environmental taxes significantly reduce emissions, suggesting their potential as effective strategies for transport decarbonization. Heterogeneity analysis reveals lower debt thresholds for low-growth and politically unstable economies. Overall, by integrating fiscal and transport sustainability within a unified theoretical framework, this study provides novel evidence and practical policy insights for designing debt-sustainable, climate-aligned transport strategies.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: How do temperature and precipitation influence electric vehicle adoption? Evidence from U.S. States
Authors: Fengxiu Zhang, Yuzheng Xie, David W.S. Wong, Wenying Ji
Abstract: Although extensive technical evidence shows that temperature and precipitation affect electric vehicle (EV) performance, less is known about how these factors translate to adoption behavior. This study examines how temperature and precipitation – incorporating both average and extreme conditions – shape EV adoption. Using panel data from 2016 to 2023 on the 48 contiguous U.S. states and the District of Columbia, we find that mean annual temperature exhibits a positive and linear relationship with EV uptake. Mean annual precipitation has no standalone effect but weakens the influence of mean temperature. Among extreme conditions, only low-temperature days (below 10°C) reduce EV adoption, while high-temperature days (above 25°C) show no significant effect. The effects of extreme precipitation are context-dependent: it promotes adoption under high-temperature conditions but shows no significant effect in cold environments. The study highlights the need for climate-sensitive and regionally tailored strategies to promote EVs and offers actionable policy recommendations.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Unveiling amplified socioeconomic disparities in electric vehicle charging infrastructure: Accessibility versus utilization
Authors: Changlong Ling, Peng Chen
Abstract: This study examines user-centered spatial disparities in electric vehicle charging infrastructure by jointly analyzing accessibility (equity) and utilization (efficiency) in Shenzhen, China. It investigates how disparities differ between the two measures, and which factors explain utilization patterns. Using charging-station data, socioeconomic disparities are quantified across income and migrant groups, and a GeoXAI approach identifies nonlinear and spatially heterogeneous relationships. Results show that disparities exist under both measures but are consistently larger during utilization. From accessibility to utilization, Gini coefficients increase by 1.1%–3.4% and Theil indices by 3.0%–9.5%. Charging stations in areas with larger low-income populations exhibit higher energy use, while those in areas with higher migrant shares are associated with longer charging durations and higher occupancy rates. Infrastructure, pricing, and built environment factors are correlated with utilization, with strong nonlinearity and spatial heterogeneity. These findings underscore utilization-aware charging evaluations and user-centered infrastructure planning.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Collaborative planning framework for heavy-duty truck electrification: corridor-port integrated energy systems
Authors: Ruihua Wang, Xuejun Feng, Suyang Wang, Kaixuan Tao, Yan Zhang, Kum Fai Yuen, Min Wu
Abstract: Deep decarbonisation of heavy-duty truck freight is essential for global carbon neutrality. As vital intermodal hubs, ports can support the development of green freight corridors. However, existing research on port integrated energy systems primarily focuses on internal logistics and vessels, neglecting corridor- port energy-demand coupling. To bridge this gap, we propose a “Corridor-Port Integrated Energy System” (C-PIES) framework and develop a two-stage distributionally robust optimisation model to address uncertainties in renewable energy generation and freight traffic flow. Using high-frequency GPS trajectory data, ambiguity sets are constructed to support robust scheduling of port renewable energy for corridor traffic-driven loads. A case study of Quanzhou Port shows that C-PIES enables source-load-storage coordination through battery swapping stations reducing system cost by 42.89% and carbon emissions by 50.2% compared with the isolated mode. The results demonstrate the potential of ports as regional energy hubs for low-carbon freight corridors.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Port environmental health Risks: Insights from the Tarragona Port-Industrial complex and planning implications
Authors: Jose L. Domingo, Joaquim Rovira, Martí Nadal
Abstract: Ports handle approximately 80% of world trade and concentrate vessels, cargo operations, and logistics that generate substantial pollution affecting nearby populations. Following a structured literature search and a narrative synthesis organized around a source-to-exposure-to-impact conceptual framework, this review evaluates the health risks associated with residential proximity to ports. Evidence consistently links port-related emissions to cardiovascular and respiratory mortality, asthma, lung cancer, adverse pregnancy outcomes, and neurodevelopmental effects. The Tarragona Port is used as an illustrative example of a complex port-industrial setting in which port and co-located petrochemical emissions jointly contribute to a quantified local burden of preventable deaths and disability-adjusted life years, although the fraction attributable to port activities alone cannot be readily isolated from that of the adjacent petrochemical complex and other urban sources. These findings support targeted interventions, including mandatory Health Impact Assessments, health-based buffer zones, optimized freight routing, and real-time air quality monitoring integrated into port operations.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Route efficiency and carbon emissions of commercial UAV delivery: Evidence from Shenzhen
Authors: Jing-Peng Wang, Yong Zhou, Yang Cui, Qiong Tian, Peng Liu
Abstract: Urban commercial unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) delivery is increasingly regarded as a faster and potentially lower-emission alternative to ground-based logistics, yet direct evidence from repeated operations remains scarce. Using commercial telemetry from Shenzhen in 2024, this study empirically characterizes an operational UAV delivery network. We retain 45,256 valid trajectories to examine network structure and route performance. Operations are concentrated on recurrent origin-destination (OD) corridors. Compared with OSRM-routed ground alternatives between matched rounded endpoints, the mean trajectory-level route-saving ratio is 15.78%, and the mean absolute distance saving is 1.08 km per delivery. We then translate the observed route records into scenario-based operational carbon estimates. Under the baseline coefficients, estimated UAV operational emissions are 0.080 kg CO 2 per delivery, compared with 0.243 kg CO 2 per delivery for electric vehicle and 1.022 kg CO 2 per delivery for fuel vehicle. UAV trajectories are observed, whereas ground routes and emissions are modeled under stated assumptions. The results provide an empirical basis for selective UAV deployment in urban logistics planning.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Research on new energy vehicle diffusion via multi-subsidy trade-in policy analysis
Authors: Yu’e Wu, Zeyun Liu, Xinyu Wang, Anran Yin, Shuhua Zhang
Abstract: The development of new energy vehicles (NEVs) has become one of China’s pivotal strategic initiatives for achieving low-carbon goals. Considering the renewal and further implementation of the vehicle trade-in policy in 2025, this research establishes a system dynamics model based on evolutionary game theory to analyze the market evolution of NEVs under multiple subsidy mechanisms. Through numerical simulations and sensitivity analysis, we investigate how critical model parameters influence the system, including multiple subsidies under trade-in policies, the initial strategy proportions of various stakeholders, and the composition of different consumer segments. The results demonstrate that under the current multi-subsidy mechanism, consumers ultimately show a clear trend toward participating in trade-in programs. Moreover, subsidies provided by enterprises to trade-in consumers exert a pronounced positive effect in promoting green automotive consumption. The policy recommendations proposed in this study provide clear directions for China’s NEV market amid the emerging wave of vehicle trade-in program.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Beyond connectivity: Travel behavior and hidden inequities in human mobility resilience
Authors: Jingke Hong, Bingsheng Liu, Ran Wei, Yang Jia, Chengchen Guo
Abstract: As climate-related extreme events intensify in frequency and severity, sustaining access to employment, healthcare, and other essential activities increasingly depends on the resilience of human mobility. This study advances mobility-resilience assessment by explicitly incorporating behavioral constraints that shape how travelers adapt under disruption. While conventional approaches largely equate resilience with transportation network connectivity, we conceptualize resilience as a behaviorally grounded outcome that depends on whether technically feasible trips remain acceptable within travelers’ limited tolerance for disruption-induced detours. Using large-scale mobile phone origin–destination data from Chongqing, China, we develop a behaviorally informed framework that integrates empirically estimated detour tolerance into resilience measurement, enabling the quantification of functional mobility loss under flood-induced network disruption. Results show that ignoring travel behavior systematically overestimates realized mobility resilience and masks critical spatial and social inequities, with low-income populations exhibiting consistently lower mobility resilience, particularly under more severe climate scenarios.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Damping-enhanced tire-pavement noise mitigation of thermoplastic polyurethane/crumb rubber composite-modified asphalt pavements
Authors: Zehua Zhu, Keke Lou, Peng Xiao, Jun Zhou, Chenying Li
Abstract: Road traffic noise is a major environmental burden of urban transport, and tire-pavement interaction is a key source-control pathway. This study developed a damping-oriented noise-mitigation strategy for SMA-13 mixtures prepared with thermoplastic polyurethane/crumb rubber (TPU/CR) composite-modified binders. Laboratory damping and acoustic tests were combined with a coupled tire-pavement-air finite element model incorporating explicit tread patterns to link material damping, vibration attenuation, and transition in the dominant noise source. The results showed that TPU/CR modification enhanced the critical damping ratio, with the optimum response obtained at 6 wt% TPU + 10 wt% CR, representing an increase of up to 14.46% over the CR-modified mixture. Enhanced damping promoted viscoelastic energy dissipation and reduced vibration-induced sound pressure levels. Simulations revealed a speed-dependent transition: vibration noise dominated at 60–90 km/h, whereas air-pumping noise became the main contributor above 90 km/h. TPU/CR modification therefore provides a damping-oriented source-control strategy for reducing tire-pavement noise while maintaining pavement performance.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Policy pathways for low-carbon transport in Ireland: Carbon taxes and ICE bans
Authors: Daniel Cassidy, Kelly de Bruin
Abstract: This paper develops I3E-Transport, a new Irish passenger transport model that integrates behavioural, technological, and macroeconomic drivers to assess the effectiveness of carbon taxation and internal combustion engine (ICE) phase-out policies on emissions from private cars and public transport. The model is soft linked to the Ireland Environment-Energy-Economy (I3E) CGE framework, allowing for a comprehensive evaluation of how these policy measures influence transport demand, vehicle stock composition, energy consumption and emissions within the passenger transport sector. Simulations for 2024–2050 indicate that, under a business-as-usual scenario, emissions rise by 2050 despite modest gains in energy efficiency and alternative vehicle uptake. A carbon tax yields only limited abatement, whereas a comprehensive ICE ban from 2035—banning hybrids—reduces CO 2 emissions by over five million tonnes relative to the baseline by 2050. However, the results show that the sector remains off track relative to implied carbon budget ceilings under a 2035 implementation, with only an earlier and comprehensive ban delivering substantial progress towards compliance, pointing to the need for timely and coordinated policy action to align Ireland’s transport sector with its long-term climate commitments.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Typhoon and bike-sharing: Non-linear built environment associations with activity recovery in Shenzhen
Authors: Yi Long, Haoran Jiang, Shaozhi Hong, Yangyang Su
Abstract: With extreme weather becoming more frequent, transportation resilience is critical. However, evidence remains limited regarding how built-environment and urban-context conditions are associated with grid-level bike-sharing activity recovery under disruption. We analyze dockless bike-sharing recovery during Typhoon Cempaka in Shenzhen using Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), Generalized Additive Model (GAM), and model-based 3D response surfaces. The outcome captures service-use recovery, not individual cycling safety, welfare, or causal resilience. Results show that: (1) nighttime light intensity, population density, and distance to the nearest planned urban functional center are the leading diagnostic predictors; (2) several predictors show non-linear fitted responses, so recovery associations vary by range; and (3) the strongest interaction patterns connect activity intensity with population concentration, polycentric location, and transit accessibility. Robustness checks indicate sensitivity to baseline demand and meteorological exposure, and spatial validation shows residual spatial structure.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Financing constraints and structural drivers of maritime decarbonization
Authors: Jau Yang Liu
Abstract: Maritime transport accounts for nearly 3% of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet decarbonization research often assumes that stronger regulation will automatically accelerate transition. This study examines how financial, technological, and regulatory conditions jointly shape the feasibility of capital mobilization in shipping. Using integrated factor extraction, perception-based causal mapping (DEMATEL), and Importance–Performance Analysis (IPA), the study identifies perceived structural interdependencies influencing maritime decarbonization finance. The results suggest that financial viability, liquidity conditions, risk-sharing mechanisms, and digital verification infrastructure are perceived as key enabling conditions, while regulatory and stakeholder factors tend to operate as reinforcing elements. Rather than indicating regulatory insufficiency, the findings highlight the interdependence between policy signals and financial-system readiness. This study contributes by integrating structural diagnostics with prioritization logic and provides policy-relevant insights for sequencing interventions in capital-intensive transport systems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Evaluating railway pressure on ecological corridors: From local disturbance to network-level risk
Authors: Yutian Liu, Zhengying Liu
Abstract: Railways increasingly affect ecological corridors that support landscape connectivity and species movement, with effects that can include both negative and context-dependent positive influences. Existing studies mainly focus on local effects such as crossings, fragmentation, and barriers, while system-level understanding of railway ecological pressure remains limited. To address this, we developed a local-to-network simulation framework to examine how segment-level railway ecological pressure is organized and how it relates to ecological network resilience loss. The results show that railway ecological pressure is spatially limited but strongly concentrated in a small subset of segments. Among them, some segments generate substantial network-level resilience loss, with different forms including structural, functional, and coupled decline. Regular and high-speed railways also exhibit distinct ecological resilience-risk organizations, indicating different modes through which railway disturbance can affect ecological corridors. These findings provide a basis for identifying priority segments for ecological mitigation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Economic implications of EVs in Europe: A scenario analysis of value added
Authors: Timm Hoefer
Abstract: The transition from internal combustion engine vehicles to electric vehicles changes where value is captured in the automotive supply chain. This study introduces a vehicle-level model of passenger cars (2020–2032), linking global production data, price breakdowns, and trade flows to map gross value added across eleven value chain segments. The results show that, in 2024, the European Union captures a 12.9 percentage point lower share of gross value added from battery electric vehicles than from comparable internal combustion engine vehicles. If this gap persists in the 2032 fleet, the implied shortfall is €3,575 per vehicle. Across 2032 value chain configurations, European Union outcomes range from −€92 billion to +€63 billion relative to baseline, with local assembly and battery manufacturing as the largest levers. The study shows how the electric vehicle transition reallocates value creation across components, regions, and firm ownership, offering a granular view of Europe’s industrial and regional exposure.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Tracking walking change post-relocation: A big data quasi-experiment of built environment effects
Authors: Nuoxian Huang, Daming Lu, Wenbo Guo, Wenjia Zhang
Abstract: Understanding how changes in built environment (BE) affect walking behavior remains a central issue in transport research. Residential relocation offers a useful quasi-experimental setting, yet post-relocation behavioral adjustment process is largely unknown. Using year-long daily mobile-phone data from relocators in Shenzhen, this study combines Interrupted Time Series (ITS) and comparative ITS with propensity score matching to estimate both immediate and gradual effects of BE changes on walking distance. Our results reveal temporal dynamics after relocation. Higher road network density, subway density, and open space consistently promote walking, whereas land use mix shows only an initial positive effect and population density and bus stop density show only gradual effects. The study extends conventional before-and-after relocation approaches by leveraging high-frequency longitudinal data to provide a more nuanced and complete picture of BE effects. These findings highlight the importance of adopting flexible, context-sensitive and temporally informed perspectives in transport planning and policy evaluation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Corrigendum to “Bridging socio-physical impacts, restoration efficacy and neighborhoods’ social vulnerability facing road flooding” [Transp. Res. Part D 159 (2026) 105506]
Authors: Jie Jiang, Yifan Yang, Yongsheng Yang, Weiping Wang, Jingkong Hong, S. Thomas Ng
Abstract: The authors regret that the affiliation of Yifan Yang was incorrectly listed in the published article. The correct affiliation is updated as above. This correction concerns the author affiliation only and does not affect the scientific content, results, conclusions, or interpretations of the article. The authors would like to apologise for any inconvenience caused.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Measuring carbon mitigation potential from a network perspective: Evidence from Changsha
Authors: Dazhi Zhao, Pu Wang, Rihong Ke, Qi Liu, Ling Liu
Abstract: Promoting green travel is essential to reducing transportation-related carbon emissions, yet evidence remains limited on how to identify neighborhoods that should be prioritized for decarbonization and how to design effective policy packages. Using Changsha, China, as a case study, we integrate mobile phone data with license plate recognition data to estimate green travel demand and construct travel-related carbon emission networks to assess neighborhood-level carbon mitigation potential. We then apply an XGBoost model with SHAP analysis to examine how built-environment factors shape this potential and to design spatially differentiated policy packages. The findings reveal a clear center-periphery gradient in carbon mitigation potential. Central urban areas should be targeted with travel demand management measures, whereas peripheral areas require strengthened infrastructure. The proposed framework quantifies differences in carbon mitigation potential across urban neighborhoods and provides a basis for deploying customized low-carbon transport policies.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: No remote, hybrid remote, and full remote: Additional insights from telework intensity
Authors: Peng Chen, Changlong Ling
Abstract: This study investigates the factors of telework intensity, no telework, hybrid telework, and full telework, using a generalized ordered logit model. The analysis integrates commuting characteristics, employer-based travel demand management strategies, and industry/occupation factors. Results indicate that telework intensity is primarily associated with occupational characteristics, workplace policies, and commuting conditions. Knowledge-intensive industries exhibit substantially higher levels of telework participation, whereas socio-demographic and built-environment factors contribute limited explanatory power. Elasticity analysis shows that automobile dependence significantly decreases the probability of teleworking, while longer in-vehicle travel time is negatively associated with higher telework intensity. Among employer-based strategies, flextime significantly increases telework participation, whereas compressed workweeks function as a substitute. These findings highlight the dominant role of job-related constraints and workplace flexibility in shaping telework intensity and illuminate the importance of differentiating telework participation by intensity level.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Roadside native species seeding practices of Midwestern US departments of transportation
Authors: Wesley J. Bollinger, Rabin Bhattarai, Jeffrey W. Matthews
Abstract: To counteract environmental problems associated with road construction and maintenance, road agencies have developed vegetation management plans that incorporate native seeding. We reviewed the specifications manuals from the Departments of Transportation of eight US states to synthesize information on native plant species used, seed mixes, site preparation, seeding methods, and maintenance to provide recommendations for roadside vegetation management. Manuals varied among states in terms of the species composition and functional diversity of plants listed for use. Individual mixes included an average of 14 native species, although some had as few as 3, and many lacked functional diversity or early blooming forbs that would benefit pollinators. We identified several early-blooming, low-cost, conservative plant species that could be incorporated into seed mixes. Compared to other states, Minnesota listed more native species and seed mixes, and provided detailed specifications for seeding, establishment, and maintenance, aligning well with recommendations based on ecological restoration research.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: The Wheel of Satisfaction: Cyclists’ perceptions and environmental Mindsets
Authors: Marc Prieto, Barbara Caemmerer, Dejan Glavas, Jean-Sébastien Lacam, Marjorie Tendero
Abstract: Despite extensive research on active mobility, determinants of cycling satisfaction remain underexplored, though satisfaction is crucial for promoting cycling and shaping policy. This study proposes and tests an integrative model grounded in Experienced Utility Theory, incorporating safety and security perceptions, habits, mobility patterns, and psychological factors such as perceived benefits and environmental concerns. Environmental attitudes are assessed using the New Ecological Paradigm (NEP) scale, rarely applied in transport research. Based on a representative sample of the French population (N = 1,028), we conduct a confirmatory factor analysis and estimate linear regressions on a sub-sample of 365 cyclists. The results indicate that core perceptions, namely safety, convenience, and enjoyment, are strongly associated with cycling satisfaction. Cyclists who attribute environmental damage to human action report significantly higher satisfaction, whereas recognition of planetary limits is not significantly associated with satisfaction.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Heterogeneous shipping companies’ responses under emissions trading schemes: An equilibrium analysis
Authors: Lerong Xu, Xi Lin, Xiwen Bai
Abstract: Emissions Trading Schemes (ETS) are pivotal for decarbonizing the shipping industry. This study develops an equilibrium framework to characterize the strategic responses of heterogeneous shipping companies to an ETS, jointly incorporating ship speed and green investment decisions with the price of carbon emission allowances (CEAs) determined endogenously through market clearing. We establish the existence and uniqueness of equilibrium under mild conditions. Theoretical analysis reveals that larger companies naturally operate at lower speeds and achieve lower per-ship emissions. These size-dependent patterns are broadly consistent with empirical evidence from the EU Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) system. Numerical experiments further demonstrate that green investment remains size-neutral when revenue losses from speed reduction are moderate. Moreover, markets with a higher proportion of small companies exhibit elevated equilibrium CEA prices under identical emission caps. These findings provide critical insights into heterogeneous company behavior and support more effective ETS policy design for maritime transport.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Bayesian copula–stochastic programming for K-ETS carbon cost endogenization in Korean rail freight
Authors: Yong-Jae Lee
Abstract: This study develops a two-stage stochastic wagon-allocation framework that endogenizes carbon costs under the Korea Emissions Trading Scheme (K-ETS), integrating hierarchical Bayesian demand reconstruction with a Student-t copula to capture correlated freight-demand uncertainty. Four contributions are reported. First, Bayesian–copula integration reduces posterior uncertainty bands by 60–85% for small-sample commodities. Second, carbon-cost endogenization yields a Value of the Stochastic Solution (VSS) of KRW 0.35 billion/year, a 17.9% improvement over the deterministic benchmark (EEV = KRW 1.96 billion), while reducing CO 2 equivalent (CO 2 e) emissions by 6.7%, indicating sustainability and competitiveness are mutually reinforcing. Third, grid carbon-intensity recalibration (2010–2024) identifies a 2021 structural inflection point (−15.8% grams CO 2 e per gross tonne-kilometre) overlooked by static-emission approaches. Fourth, the stochastic-planning advantage holds across six K-ETS price scenarios and competitive-response assumptions, confirming policy invariance. Bounded to short-term optimization by Korea’s 29.8% rail-freight demand contraction through 2023, the framework transfers to markets under active emissions trading regimes.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Barriers to sustainable urban air mobility: A hybrid method perspective
Authors: Ziyi Wu, Jianghong Feng
Abstract: Against the backdrop of increasingly severe urban ground traffic congestion and pollution, urban air mobility represented by electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft has emerged as a highly promising solution. However, the large-scale deployment of eVTOL still faces numerous barriers. Thus, this paper aims to identify twenty-three key barriers influencing eVTOL adoption through a literature review and expert interviews. The study then examines their interrelationships and hierarchical structure through the decision-making trial and evaluation laboratory and interpretive structural modeling methods. The result indicates that these twenty-three barriers can be categorized into six levels, with the lack of airworthiness standards and inconsistencies and low-altitude airspace restriction representing the highest-level barriers. Moreover, the combined influence of operational and economic barriers is an important consideration. This paper has enriched the understanding of barriers to eVTOL adoption, providing guidance for policy makers and key decision-makers to promote the sustainable development of urban transportation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: How do non-emergency medical transportation services influence patients’ subjective well-being?
Authors: Maryam Yousefibaseri, Yi-Ling Cheng, Jane Lin
Abstract: Subjective well-being (SWB) related to travel experience has been a growing area of interest in transportation research, particularly through the mediating effects of travel satisfaction. While prior studies have extensively examined this relationship in the context of commuting and leisure travel, the role of non-emergency medical transportation (NEMT) service quality in shaping SWB remains underexplored. These trips present unique challenges such as physical vulnerability, time sensitivity, and emotional stress. This study investigates how user perceptions of NEMT service quality influence service satisfaction and SWB using survey data collected among rural patients in Illinois. The results indicate that reliability is the most influential factor affecting service satisfaction; reservation technology, customer service, accessibility, and driver behavior also contribute significantly to satisfaction with NEMT, and subsequently SWB. These findings underscore the critical importance of reliable and user-friendly NEMT services in supporting patients’ well-being and shed light on how to improve NEMT systems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Regulating the service: A cargo-loading credit trading scheme for shipping decarbonization
Authors: Xiaoyi Shen, Ying Kou, Mengchi Li
Abstract: Market-based measures (MBMs) for shipping decarbonization remain inadequate because most existing approaches regulate how ships operate rather than what they deliver. This study proposes a cargo-loading credit trading scheme (CL CTS), a novel baseline-and-credit MBM that adopts an output-based baseline linked to cargo transported. To assess the scheme, we first model ship-level and fleet-level decisions under an open trading system and compare the CL CTS with a ship-efficiency credit trading scheme. Under the same emission budget, the CL CTS achieves greater emission reductions at lower compliance costs by uniformly incentivizing speed reduction across all vessels. We further extend the model to aclosed, sector-wide system covering the global fleet of vessels. The CL CTS admits a unique and predictable equilibrium, allowing credit prices and total emissions to be controlled through policy standards. Overall, this service-based CL CTS offers a better policy choice for shipping to decarbonize.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Comparative energy consumption analysis of electric and hydrogen buses using real-world data
Authors: Xiaokuan Zhao, Zhicheng Jin, Weihua Gu, Wenbo Fan, Chi Xie
Abstract: This study provides a model-based empirical comparison of real-world energy consumption for a double-decker battery-electric bus (DDEB) and a double-decker hydrogen fuel-cell bus (DDHB) in the same urban context. It fills two gaps in prior studies: scarce real-world DDHB models and limited granular comparisons on double-decker platforms. Using route, vehicle-status, weather, and traffic features, we evaluated five prediction models. Best-performing models achieved mean absolute percentage errors of 12.16% for the DDEB and 11.85% for the DDHB. Average energy use was 1.770 kWh/km for the DDEB and 0.120 kg H 2 -eq/km (4.011 kWh-eq/km) for the DDHB. Multi-model SHAP results identified ambient temperature, mean speed, stop intensity, and passenger load as important predictors for both buses. Initial battery state of charge was more important for the DDHB, consistent with the buffering role of its auxiliary battery. Results support route planning and energy management for double-decker zero-emission buses.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Horizontal evacuation dynamics of pedestrians during urban flooding: Insights from straight-corridor experiments
Authors: Chenglin Guo, Xintong Li, Jinghui Wang, Jun Zhang, Weiguo Song
Abstract: Urban flooding events occur frequently, posing severe challenges to public safety. This study focuses on horizontal evacuation, systematically investigating pedestrian dynamics during urban flooding using a large-scale, high-fidelity experimental platform. Through straight-corridor experiments under varying hydraulic conditions, the adaptive behavioral mechanisms of pedestrians are examined from the perspectives of macroscopic flow, microscopic motion, and collective interaction. The results indicate that hydrodynamic effects on crowd flow capacity exhibit significant density dependence: at low densities, water resistance dominates, whereas at medium-to-high densities, collective adaptation emerges. Microscopic analysis reveals that wading conditions alter pedestrians’ gait regulation mechanisms, with individuals tending to adopt compensatory strategies to maintain locomotion stability. Additionally, pedestrians exhibit tendencies of cooperative behavior, which may contribute to reduced hydrodynamic loads through closer spacing and utilization of wake regions behind others. This study provides empirical evidence for pedestrian evacuation under urban flooding and offers valuable support for evacuation modeling and emergency management.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Subsidy pass-through and policy optimization for port drayage truck electrification under vehicle-leasing
Authors: Hongzhi Miao, Shumin Li, Xinwei Li, Jianfeng Zheng
Abstract: Port drayage trucks are a priority segment for freight decarbonization given their concentrated emissions and favorable duty cycles. Under the vehicle leasing model, government subsidies must propagate through a hierarchical market structure where intermediary pricing can attenuate policy effectiveness. Prior works rarely model subsidy pass-through as endogenous to operator pricing, or quantify its coupling with charging congestion. This study develops a three-tier bilevel Stackelberg game with embedded market equilibrium to quantify pass-through efficiency and identify welfare-maximizing policy portfolios. Results show that: (1) Driver subsidies achieve 95% end-user transmission by bypassing operator pricing, whereas purchase subsidies attain only 55% due to profit-maximizing markup adjustments. (2) Charging infrastructure imposes a critical utilization threshold near 70%, beyond which queuing delays constrain fleet electrification. (3) The optimal portfolio prioritizes driver subsidies, complemented by tax exemptions and infrastructure investment, generating a synergy coefficient of 1.70. Sensitivity analysis confirms structural robustness while point estimates remain calibration-dependent.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: How L2 intelligent-driving configuration diffusion is associated with urban carbon emission intensity
Authors: Zhexin Zhu, Feiyu Chen, Xiaoguang Yang
Abstract: As vehicle electrification and intelligent driving advance worldwide, carbon effects of intelligent-driving configurations in new energy vehicles (NEVs) remain unclear. Using panel data for 272 cities from 2018 to 2024, this study examines the relationship between L2 intelligent-driving configuration diffusion in NEVs (IDNEV) and urban carbon emission intensity (CEI). Results show that higher IDNEV is positively associated with CEI: a 1 percentage point increase in IDNEV is associated with an additional 69.9 tonnes of CO 2 per 100 million yuan of GDP. Vehicle energy consumption serves as a vehicle-composition energy channel linking IDNEV and CEI. Threshold results reveal that the relationship between IDNEV and CEI is context-dependent: the positive association strengthens with green and intelligent innovation capacity and shifts from negative to positive as population agglomeration rises. Spatially, IDNEV is positively associated with local CEI but negatively associated with CEI in neighbouring cities, contributing to lower regional CEI.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Techno-economic analysis of HGV trailer tyres based on wear and fuel consumption
Authors: Chen Liu, Parth Deshpande, Xiaoxiang Na, David Cebon
Abstract: Fuel consumption and tyre replacement are two important factors influencing the total cost of ownership (TCO) of heavy goods vehicles (HGV). Low rolling resistance (RR) tyres reduce fuel consumption but typically experience higher wear, increasing replacement costs. This study presents a comparative techno-economic analysis of conventional and low RR tyres using a tyre wear model and vehicle energy consumption model across long-haul, urban, and mixed-use operations. The effect of trailer steering systems, which reduce tyre scrubbing, is also assessed. Results show that without steering system, low RR tyres reduce TCO only in long-haul and mixed-use scenarios, while conventional tyres remain more economical in urban driving. Trailer steering systems enable low RR tyres to achieve lowest TCO in all scenarios, while providing a total saving of £35,000 over trailer service life for urban operations. Combining trailer steering and low RR tyres can reduce the operational cost by 4.9% for mixed-use operations.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Exploring metro station ridership: the role of network attraction and factor interactions
Authors: Lu Zhao, Wenfei Zhao, Rui Li, Zijia Wang, Linmu Zou, Feng Chen, Yizhe Wang
Abstract: With accelerating urbanization, understanding the mechanisms shaping metro station ridership is crucial for optimizing service planning. Metro ridership analysis is challenged by spatial heterogeneity and nonlinear factor interactions. This study integrates Multiscale Geographically Weighted Regression with the Geographical Detector to reveal ridership patterns across station types. A multi-level “station–network” factor system is built by combining station attributes with attraction factors, and K-means++ is used to classify stations into residential, employment, and mixed types. GeoDetector quantifies individual and interaction effects, with the strongest interactions embedded into the MGWR model to uncover how these factors jointly determine ridership variations. Results from Beijing show that attraction factors and their interactions significantly improve model performance. Ridership at residential-dominant stations is mainly influenced by accessibility, employment-intensive stations by land use attributes, and mixed-function stations by multi-level interactions among service, commercial, and population. Findings provide insights for ridership mechanisms and guide metro planning.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Travel satisfaction across public transport journey chain stages: Evidence from mobility-impaired individuals
Authors: Shuai Yuan, Esther Hiu Kwan Yung, Yujun Fan, Siqiang Wang, Xiaojie Du
Abstract: Mobility impaired travel involves barriers throughout a journey, but quantitative evaluation of satisfaction with each journey stage remains scarce. We analyzed travel satisfaction with a public transport chain among 392 people with mobility impairments in Hong Kong. Using confirmatory factor analysis, we developed and validated a framework comprising three dimensions in built environment (e.g., first-mile connectivity) and four in public transport (e.g., transport stops, transfers). Satisfaction with public transport dimensions was lower than the built environment. Compared with the new-town rural area, the metro area received lower satisfaction with the built environment, due to street crossings and distances to stops. Overall satisfaction related most strongly to transport service usability and first-mile connectivity in the metro area and the new town-rural areas, respectively. However, journey dimensions disconnected with objective environment measures (e.g., transit stop density). Future research may expand public transport journey chain to include door-to-building exit transition and destination activities.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Rise, stagnation, and resurgence of hybrid electric vehicles in the U.S. market
Authors: Chang (Charo) Liu, Jax T. Fisher, John German, John D. Graham
Abstract: This article examines the rise, stagnation, and resurgence of the conventional (strong) hybrid electric vehicle (HEV) in the United States from 1999 to 2025. We investigate two research questions: (1) Why has there been a resurgence of consumer and manufacturer interest in HEVs? (2) Is this resurgence coming at the expense of battery electric vehicles (BEVs) or conventional internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles? Drawing on case studies, policy analysis, payback-period calculations, and a statistical analysis of vehicle registration microdata from the State of New York, we find that product innovation—lower price premiums, improved performance, and no sacrifice in cargo space—is the primary driver of the HEV resurgence, which has occurred despite the absence of direct federal or state purchase incentives. The statistical analysis shows that HEV market share gains in New York have come predominantly at the expense of conventional ICE vehicles, while the estimated relationships with BEV and PHEV shares are much smaller and less consistent across samples. These findings suggest that, in markets like New York at current penetration levels, HEVs and plug-in electric vehicles are more complementary than directly substitutive in the transition to lower-carbon transportation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Uncrewed aircraft system base site suitability analysis for multi-hazard disaster response
Authors: Lhiana Reign S. Bañares, Adriana Andreeva-Mori
Abstract: Integrating Uncrewed Aircraft Systems (UAS) for search-and-rescue (SAR) enhances disaster risk reduction (DRR), yet technical and topographical constraints limit efficacy. This study proposes a pragmatic, multi-hazard framework combining geospatial analysis and mathematical optimization for strategic pre-disaster base planning. We evaluated site suitability by integrating evacuation facilities, multi-hazard exposure, slope, and land use data. Applied to Japan’s Mt. Unzen region, prone to landslides and tsunamis, the methodology identified optimal UAS base zones across diverse seasonal scenarios. Results demonstrate that flexible base selection maximizes risk-weighted coverage. Furthermore, while extending UAS operational range improves coverage, marginal benefits diminish beyond a specific threshold. These findings provide DRR practitioners and drone operators with a structured framework for pre-disaster positioning, significantly improving the efficiency and reach of emergency response operations. This integrated model bridges the gap between single-hazard studies and real-world multi-hazard complexity, offering actionable insights for strategic disaster preparedness and rapid SAR deployment.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Corrigendum to “Data-driven analysis of EV public charging station demand across heterogeneous built environment” [Transp. Res. Part D: Transp. Environ. 158 (2026) 105455]
Authors: Junfang Tian, Shuo Li, Kun Wang, Zhenjie Zheng, Qianran Zhang
Abstract: The authors regret that the affiliations of Kun Wang and Qianran Zhang were incorrectly assigned in the published version of the article. The correct affiliations are updated as above.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Redefining empty trips through occupancy and transferability of cross-modal strategies: A review
Authors: Pedram Akbari, Gonçalo Homem de Almeida Correia, Merkebe Getachew Demissie
Abstract: Empty trips, vehicle movements without payload, generate unsustainable externalities. This study addresses these challenges by identifying shortcomings in the literature on empty trip generation across all modes through a combined narrative and systematic review. The review revealed that the conventional definition of empty trips adopts a binary empty/non-empty perspective, which fails to capture the extent of the problem. In response, we propose a continuous measure based on the proportion of unused vehicle capacity. Our review also reveals that mitigation strategies are often case-specific, which limits their impact and transferability across modes. To address this limitation, we introduce a framework that facilitates the transferability of strategies by highlighting cross-modal similarities in generating empty trips. Finally, we reviewed these strategies, their methodologies, and the associated problems related to empty trips using the systematic review in driver-provided mobility, which includes public transportation, carpooling, taxi, and ride-hailing to support sustainable mobility through strategy generalization.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Public transit and shared micromobility bundles: Contrasting stated preferences and actual sales
Authors: Matthias Brüning
Abstract: Bundles and mobility-as-a-service (MaaS) plans are seen as promising instruments to integrate shared electric micromobility with public transit, yet evidence on effective designs and their real-world uptake remains scarce. In a first step, we use a stated choice experiment among Swiss residents ( n = 1 , 422 across two samples) and estimate mixed logit models to assess preferences for three subscription bundle types (flat rates, 50% discount passes, minute packages) and single-journey bundles. In a second step, we compare the model-implied market shares with sales data from a 10-week pilot in Eastern Switzerland. Prior experience of shared micromobility services emerged as the dominant predictor of bundle utility. We document a substantial gap between stated preference and adoption: only 2.4-4.6% of hypothetical interest translates into purchases. Despite this gap, the sales compare favorably to previous MaaS trials. The results imply that practitioners should anticipate considerably lower uptake than is indicated by survey-based projections.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Timing matters: shifts in traffic intensity impact the risk of wildlife-vehicle collisions
Authors: Johanna Heeres, Manisha Bhardwaj, Falko Brieger
Abstract: Wildlife–vehicle collisions (WVC) result from the interaction between traffic and wildlife. While traffic is structured by clock time, wildlife activity is governed by daylight, leading to seasonal variation in their temporal overlap. Using WVC data from Germany and hourly traffic estimates, we examined how daylight-saving time (DST) alter this overlap and affect collision risk. We found that DST-induced changes in traffic intensity significantly influenced WVC rates, however, residual variation suggested deviations from a strictly proportional response across situations. In spring, the shift of traffic into dawn was associated with higher-than-expected WVC rates, a pattern consistent with seasonal increases in wildlife movement. Variation in WVC responses was more pronounced at dawn, indicating that factors beyond traffic intensity may contribute to observed patterns. DST effects on WVC, therefore, differ from patterns observed in other regions, emphasizing the importance of considering species ecology and regional conditions when informing management decisions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: A decentralized mobile charging station scheduling method using imitation learning
Authors: Tian Lei, Zhengzhuo Wang, Xiaowei Chen, Satish V. Ukkusuri, Lei Gong, Qin Luo
Abstract: With the rapid growth of electric vehicles, spatiotemporal imbalances between charging demand and supply have become increasingly pronounced. This study proposes a decentralized mobile charging station (MCS) scheduling framework that integrates imitation learning (IL) with Transformer-based strategy modeling. IL transfers expert knowledge from a centralized control strategy to guide decentralized decision-making, while the Transformer architecture effectively captures dynamic and heterogeneous charging demand patterns. Simulation experiments using real-world data from the Luohu district of Shenzhen validate the framework’s effectiveness. The proposed method achieves near-centralized performance, stable convergence, and strong generalization across multiple system scales. Even with 44% observability of the global state, decentralized agents maintain competitive performance, particularly with 20–30 MCSs. The learned strategy transfers well to different fleet sizes without retraining, supporting scalable and adaptive deployment. These results provide a concrete pathway for efficient, autonomous coordination in large-scale distributed charging networks and offer practical guidance for future EV infrastructure planning.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Will shipment consolidation effectively Foster sustainable shipping? Incentive analysis and data validation
Authors: Baozhuang Niu, Baohui Chen, Jian Dong
Abstract: Ocean shipping is cost-effective for long-distance freight but has significantly contributed to global carbon emissions. As such, how to balance sourcing cost and carbon emission reduction becomes a great challenge for international trade companies. We observe that some companies adopt shipment consolidation strategy, which is believed to be green but involves mandatory waiting time that causes delivery delays. We observe others source locally that reduce ocean shipping volume at a significantly higher sourcing cost, especially in developed markets such as the U.S. and Europe. In this study, to formulate the key trade-offs and derive the equilibrium freight shipping strategies, we investigate a three-tier supply chain model consisting of overseas/local suppliers, one ocean shipping service provider, and one retailer that buys and resells goods to developed market consumers. We find that the shipping service provider will raise prices under shipment consolidation, while cutting prices under local sourcing strategy: Totally opposite pricing behaviors. We further find that the retailer’s strategy preference reverses twice as the negative impact of delivery delay intensifies: Initially favoring shipment consolidation, then switching to local sourcing, and finally back to shipment consolidation. We reveal that it is local sourcing strategy rather than shipment consolidation that can achieve win–win situations in some sense of higher retailer profits and lower emissions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Optimization of electric vehicle charging station layout considering mobile charging vehicles
Authors: Yin Feng, Enjian Yao, Rui Zhang, Rongsheng Chen, Lexing Zhang
Abstract: Rapid electrification of urban transport requires charging systems that can accommodate pronounced spatiotemporal demand heterogeneity. This paper develops a unified welfare-oriented planning model that jointly optimizes fixed charging station (FCS) locations and capacities, mobile charging vehicle (MCV) fleet size, and multi-period dispatch under time-varying demand. Charging demand is identified from points of interest (POI) datasets using kernel density estimation (KDE). A district-level case study in Xi’an, China illustrates how fixed and mobile charging resources can be jointly planned to address spatially uneven and time-varying demand. Among the three schemes tested, the hybrid fixed-mobile scheme achieves the highest service ratio, reaching 90.99%. The model endogenizes FCS deployment, MCV fleet sizing, and multi-period mobile service coordination within a welfare-based evaluation model.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Net-zero GHG emission in shipping networks: Role of alternative fuel bunkering hubs
Authors: Wei Yim Yap, Zengqi Xiao, Zengyan Fan, Zhong Shuo Chen
Abstract: The study analyzes the role of ports as alternative fuel bunkering hubs in achieving net-zero GHG emissions in container trades. The multi-dimensional analysis provides a realistic assessment that encompasses vessel size, number of vessels, and service frequency in addition to individual vessel movements. The study covers deployed containership capacity across all major trade routes, regions, and vessel classes. Leveraging data-driven intrinsic structures, GMM clustering is used to identify cluster centroids as candidate ports for alternative fuel bunkering. The research shows that a select number of ports can exert considerable impact on decarbonization, particularly on long-haul and inter-region routes. Under the modeled hub-coverage logic, four key bunkering locations can eliminate 77.1% of CO 2 emissions in the life-cycle scenario, rising to 87.3% when additional strategically located ports are included. These results indicate that deep decarbonization in container shipping is likely to be led by a small set of high-leverage hubs on the major east–west corridors. In addition, the dispersed nature of feeder and intra-region trades calls for a more distributed bunkering approach, with electrification as a feasible strategy for emission reduction.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Planning for on-street parking lanes in an era of autonomous vehicles
Authors: Chi Feng, Jinrui Gong, Jiayi Yang, Zhenyu Mei
Abstract: The advent of autonomous vehicles (AVs) decouples parking from destination proximity, creating an opportunity to reallocate curb space. This study develops a bi-level optimization framework for planning on-street parking lanes in an AV future. The upper-level model minimizes total social cost (integrating traveler time, AV operating cost, and land opportunity value), while the lower-level captures joint user equilibrium of parking and route choices, solved via a genetic algorithm. Numerical experiments on the Sioux Falls network under three demand scenarios demonstrate that optimized layouts reduce total travel time by 8.9%–35.6% and comprehensive system cost by 4.3%–21.1%, though efficacy diminishes under high congestion. Allocation exhibits strong demand-dependency, freeing 9,394–45,953 off-street parking spaces across scenarios. Empty repositioning decreases by 15.5%–71.9%, highlighting environmental benefits. This work provides a foundational tool for designing more sustainable, resource-efficient urban transportation systems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Data-driven investigation of ship fuel consumption integrating causal inference and hierarchical analysis
Authors: Wenjie Cao, Xinjian Wang, Wei Zhang, Huanhuan Li, Siming Fang, Zaili Yang
Abstract: This study develops a data-driven analytical framework that integrates causal inference with hierarchical analysis to reveal the underlying mechanisms influencing ship fuel consumption (SFC). The framework combines multi-source data fusion, direct linear non-gaussian acyclic model-based causal discovery, and double machine learning with causal forests model to estimate Average Treatment Effects (ATEs), followed by interpretive structural modelling for hierarchical decomposition. Experimental results under the expanded DAG-derived adjustment specification indicate that Daily sailing hours has the strongest positive conditional effect on SFC (ATE = 2.058), followed by Main engine RPM with a positive but more uncertain effect estimate (ATE = 0.268). The hierarchical analysis further organises the directional-dependence network into interpretable structural levels, thereby illustrating possible multi-level transmission patterns among operational and environmental factors. This framework provides an exploratory and graph-informed analytical basis for interpreting directional dependencies and observed-covariate conditional effect patterns in SFC, offering cautious decision support for data-driven energy management. The source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/AdvMarTech/ship_fuel_consum_causalinfer .
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Revealing bridge backwater response of large wood transported by flash floods
Authors: Gaogao Fei, Xiekang Wang
Abstract: Bridges are highly vulnerable to hydraulic loading during flash floods, particularly when large wood (LW) is transported and accumulates at bridge openings, inducing backwater rise and amplifying flood risks. This study investigates the mechanisms and risks of bridge backwater formation induced by LW under unsteady flash flood conditions through a series of systematic flume experiments. The results demonstrate that the steep rising limb of flash floods rapidly mobilizes LW towards bridges. The mixed-length LW condition leads to the highest accumulation probability because structural interlocking between long and short pieces promotes the formation of stable LW accumulations. The maximum relative backwater rise is strongly and positively correlated with the LW accumulation factor. These findings provide experimental evidence to support disaster risk reduction, infrastructure resilience assessment, and bridge design improvement with an increase in extreme flash flood events.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Resilience-oriented emergency resource site optimization for an urban multi-modal public transport network
Authors: Jinqu Chen, Xiaowei Liu, Shaochuan Zhu, Deying Su, Bo Du, Yong Yin
Abstract: Optimizing the emergency resource site (ERS) in an urban multi-modal public transport network possesses practical significance to improve its resilience under disruptions. Prior studies rarely enhance the resilience of a multi-modal network in consideration of optimizing ERSs. In this study, a resilience-oriented ERS optimization approach for a multi-modal public transport network is developed by considering the influence of emergency resource types and the severity of uncertain disruptions. Comprehensive numerical experiments are conducted on a real-life network in Chengdu. Numerical results indicate that disruptions occurring at rail stations are more severe than those at bus stops. The average resilience metrics of the multi-modal and rail networks decrease by 62.22% and 86.96%, respectively, after optimizing ERSs and their service stations. Moreover, it indicates that the optimal ERS in the multi-modal network is different from that in a single-modal network. Finally, the influence of various parameters on the model performance is discussed.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Carbon compensation for international scrap steel trade through maritime carbon pricing
Authors: He Peng, Weisheng Lu, Zhikun Chen, Chunjiang An, Jianli Hao, Wenbo Zhao
Abstract: The reuse of scrap steel is critical to decarbonizing the steel industry, with maritime logistics serving as the primary conduit for global scrap redistribution. The International Maritime Organization approved the Net Zero Framework (IMO-NZF) at MEPC 83 in April 2025, establishing a draft framework for emission reduction targets and carbon costs for global shipping. This study proposes a Substitutional Offset (SO) strategy aimed at easing the early compliance pressure of sustainable waste logistics, while maintaining climate policy constraints. Supported by Monte Carlo-based probabilistic carbon accounting, the results show that SO ratio adjustments are highly sensitive across 10 major international scrap shipping corridors. The study also offers a comparative analysis with the EU Emissions Trading System (EU-ETS), providing quantitative insights into potential alignment between the two carbon pricing regimes. Overall, this research contributes to reducing implementation barriers for global maritime carbon pricing and offers climate risk guidance for the increasingly constrained global scrap steel trade.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Understanding community resilience through multilevel modeling: application to mobility disruption during flooding
Authors: Francisco Contreras, Cristina Torres-Machi
Abstract: Vulnerability and resilience indices are widely used to identify at-risk communities and guide disaster mitigation and recovery efforts. However, their empirical relationship with disaster outcomes remains unclear. This study addresses this gap by (1) proposing a methodology to evaluate the relationship between community vulnerability or resilience and disaster outcomes, and (2) illustrating the capabilities of the methodology in a specific context. The methodology is applied to analyze mobility disruptions derived from flooding, evaluating three available vulnerability and resilience indices in the United States and the sociodemographic variables used to construct them. The results indicate that the indices differ in their relationship with mobility impacts, with the Social Vulnerability Index (SoVI) showing the strongest association. Housing-related variables exhibited the strongest relationships with mobility disruption. These findings provide new insights into the relationships among vulnerability, resilience, and disaster impacts, and support efforts to prioritize communities for investments that enhance transportation infrastructure resilience.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: The effectiveness and limits of time-of-use pricing in public EV charging networks
Authors: Mingzhi Xiao, Yuki Takayama
Abstract: Time-of-use pricing is widely used to manage demand at public EV charging stations, yet evidence on when it works and through which margin remains limited. Using station-by-day-by-hour data from Shenzhen and Amsterdam, we estimate intraday price responsiveness on two margins: whether charging occurs in a station hour and, conditional on charging, delivered energy and occupancy time. A high-dimensional fixed-effects design absorbs station-by-day demand shocks and hour-of-week patterns, so identification relies on within-station, within-day price variation under scheduled tariffs.
