We find strong context dependence in adjustment channels. Shenzhen adjusts mainly through conditional intensity and occupancy, whereas Amsterdam adjusts mainly through participation. Estimated price responsiveness differs by weather: it is weaker at higher temperatures in Shenzhen and stronger for participation during rainy hours in Amsterdam. Utilization diagnostics suggest higher charger power is consistently associated with higher throughput per charger, while very local densification is often offset by substitution in dense micro-markets.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Demand-informed link criticality analysis for bridge-centric transport networks
Authors: Daniyar Kurmankhojayev, Heqing Tan, Yu Gu, Anthony Chen
Abstract: Bridges are often treated as uniquely critical assets in road networks segmented by natural barriers such as rivers, yet existing traffic assignment-based link criticality methods generally treat them as ordinary links. This overlooks an important behavioral mechanism: in bridge-centric networks, route choice is conditioned by bridge choice, and bridge choice depends on travelers’ implicit perceptions of bridge availability. Because these demand-side perceptions influence which crossings are considered feasible or attractive, ignoring them can distort network flows and alter criticality rankings for both bridges and ordinary road links. This study develops a bridge-centric link criticality analysis framework that endogenously reveals demand-side effects of bridges in road networks. Applied to the road network of Winnipeg, Canada, the framework shows that accounting for perceived bridge availability yields different criticality rankings and highlights not only the distinct functional importance of bridges but also the comparable importance of selected non-bridge links.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Vehicle energy type preferences with hydrogen fuel cell vehicles as an alternative in electrified mobility
Authors: Ning Huan, Jiaoe Wang, Toshiyuki Yamamoto, He Hao, Hanqi Zhao, Enjian Yao
Abstract: Hydrogen fuel cell vehicles (HFCVs) have emerged as a potential pathway for extending mobility electrification. In Beijing, where battery electric vehicles (BEVs) have expanded rapidly under long-standing acquisition and usage restrictions on internal combustion engine vehicles, HFCVs are being introduced into a mobility system shaped by widespread BEV adoption. Using stated preference data and a hybrid choice modelling framework, this study examines how vehicle ownership and related attitudes influence consumers’ future vehicle energy type choices. The results show that BEV ownership is positively associated with expectations towards HFCVs and represents an important source of behavioural heterogeneity. Scenario simulation results indicate that price-related factors, particularly purchase subsidies, increase HFCV uptake primarily through substitution from BEVs, whereas exemptions from acquisition and usage restrictions increase HFCV shares mainly by enhancing their competitiveness relative to conventional vehicles. Improved refuelling-related conditions further strengthen the competitiveness of HFCVs, particularly under the assumed phase-out scenarios for internal combustion engine vehicles.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Public or private? A unified demand–supply coupled framework for EV infrastructure investment
Authors: Shuhua Hong, Tianjia Yang, Yang Song, Xianbiao (XB) Hu
Abstract: Utilizing taxpayer dollars for electric vehicle (EV) charger deployments has sparked ongoing debate over the efficiency and fairness of public spending. Public agencies aim to maximize utilization and accessibility, whereas private investors prioritize profitability. This study develops a unified modeling framework that represents public-led and private-led charging station deployment as heterogeneous decision processes and solves it using a bilevel demand–supply coupling approach. The upper level compares public-led, private-led, and coexistence scenarios under a fixed government budget, while the lower level predicts station-level utilization. The two levels are iteratively coupled: supply-side siting decisions shape demand forecasts, while demand feedback updates supply through a gradient-informed spatial expansion algorithm. Results show that private-led deployment can leverage matching capital to improve utilization and profit, but may increase user charging costs and bypass some lower-income minority areas. Sensitivity analyses indicate that private-led profitability is robust to EV adoption growth but depends strongly on charging-to-purchase conversion.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: High-resolution 3D aviation carbon emission inventory: A foundation for Chinese SAF promotion
Authors: Junxiu Ran, Siqi Cai, Xiaohui Liu, Pei Yang, Linfeng Zhang
Abstract: Traditional aviation carbon emission inventories have key limitations: insufficient spatial resolution, weak representation of dynamic vertical emission profiles, and limited support for future Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) blending scenarios. These limitations restrict precise allocation of emission mitigation responsibilities and prevent high-fidelity benchmarking for SAF mitigation accounting and differentiated deployment. We develop a high-resolution 3D gridded aviation carbon model by fusing ADS-B flight tracks and ACARS fuel data. Based on the 2025 inventory, we find that emissions show a spatial pattern characterized by higher emissions in eastern China and lower emissions in; over 90% of cruise emissions concentrate at 7–11 km; and emission dynamics are driven by seasonality and holiday shocks. An asymmetric emission flight response exists under extreme weather. We propose a novel Airspace Emission Load Ratio to classify high emission provinces into hub-type and corridor-type. This inventory provides a grid-level baseline for emission allocation and supports future SAF accounting and regional deployment analysis in China.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Evolution of mobile-source-related PM2.5 and its associated impacts: Insights from emerging contributors
Authors: Junchao Zhao, Zeyu Yang, Huan Liu, Haitong Zhe Sun, Zhenyu Luo, Zhaofeng Lv, Xiaotong Wang, Lijuan Qi, Hang Yin, Yan Ding, Kebin He
Abstract: Mobile source (MS) emission control is increasingly important for achieving further air quality improvement. This study examined the atmospheric impacts of mobile-source-related PM 2.5 (MS-PM 2.5 ), with particular attention to emerging contributors, including non-exhaust emission processes and unregulated low-volatility organic compounds. From 2011 to 2019, MS-PM 2.5 concentrations in eastern China decreased by approximately 13%. However, the contribution of MS to total PM 2.5 increased by 3.5%, and non-road sources were found to pose higher environmental risks than on-road sources. Meanwhile, low-volatility organic compounds showed increasing contributions to organic aerosol formation, highlighting the growing importance of previously underrepresented emission components. Deaths attributable to PM 2.5 pollution (DAPP) from MS increased by 44.6%, and their share of total DAPP rose by 5.9%. These findings indicate that MS-related health impacts remain substantial under improving air quality conditions. Future MS control strategies should therefore place greater emphasis on non-road sources and emerging emission processes that remain poorly regulated.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Wheels of Change: Forecasting regional electric Two-Wheeler adoption in India
Authors: Harihara Subramanian Radhakrishnan, Alok Raj, Prateek Bansal
Abstract: There has been growing global interest in adopting electric vehicles (EVs) in recent years. However, limited research specifically addresses the growth of electric two-wheelers (E2Ws), particularly in emerging economies such as India. This study aims to forecast the regional adoption of E2Ws in India using the Bass model while accounting for geospatial heterogeneity. We group Indian states into four market clusters based on two factors: the size of the two-wheeler market and the maturity of E2W adoption. This helps us capture market heterogeneity while forecasting state-level E2W adoption up to 2035. We also identify key macroeconomic and structural factors influencing E2W adoption. Our findings identify investment infrastructure and human capital as exploratory predictors of E2W innovation-led adoption. Using these results, we propose a strategic prioritization framework for Government and Industry stakeholders to design targeted economic policies and incentives to promote sustained E2W adoption across different regions in India.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Bridging socio-physical impacts, restoration efficacy and neighborhoods’ social vulnerability facing road flooding
Authors: Jie Jiang, Yifan Yang, Yongsheng Yang, Weiping Wang, Jingke Hong, S. Thomas Ng
Abstract: Road transport plays an essential role in facilitating effective hazard response and recovery efforts. However, the relationships between socio-physical impacts of flooding-induced transport interruption, efficacy of intervention strategies, and neighborhoods’ social vulnerability remains under explored. This paper presents an integrated framework that bridges the socio-physical impairment of the road transport system and the restoration efficacy of post-hazard intervention strategies with social vulnerability across neighborhoods within a community. A demonstrative case study is conducted in Wanchai, Hong Kong. The results demonstrate the proposed framework’s capability to characterize neighborhoods with high socio-physical impacts and high social vulnerability. It also provides a comparative evaluation of the efficacy across alternative intervention strategies and highlights the strategy from an equity-based perspective in supporting community post-hazard recovery. The framework provides key insights for mitigating the socio-physical impacts and the derived inequity issues arising from transportation service disruptions and restoration in urban flooding.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Evacuation dynamics and socioeconomic disparities during a tropical cyclone-blackout-heatwave compound hazard event
Authors: Xin Wang, Wei Zhai, Kerry Nice, Benteng Sun, Xueyin Bai, Haoming Qin, Huanchun Huang
Abstract: The increasing frequency of compound disasters, like 2024’s Hurricane Beryl (tropical cyclone, blackouts, and extreme heat) in Texas, challenges traditional evacuation models, as the dynamics of cascading threats are poorly understood. Using aggregated, high-resolution location data and a multi-stage analytical framework, we show that cascading blackouts under extreme heat triggered a delayed but significant increase in evacuation, with outage-affected communities exhibiting daily evacuation rates 3.0 percentage points higher after landfall than comparable non-outage communities. Spatial lag analysis further indicates that evacuation responses were clustered across neighboring communities. Furthermore, Explainable Machine Learning (XGBoost-SHAP) reveals that socioeconomic factors and racial composition were stronger predictors of evacuation than outage and heat exposure. Crucially, the proportion of white residents was the most powerful positive predictor of leaving. These findings suggest that compound disasters can simultaneously stimulate evacuation while exposing deep inequalities in who is able to respond effectively, underscoring the need for equity-centered disaster planning.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Electric vehicle charging as a monthly budget: portfolio preferences across working Americans
Authors: Amin Akbari, Katherine E. Asmussen, Matthew D. Dean
Abstract: We examine electric vehicle (EV) charging location preferences by investigating how drivers allocate monthly charging sessions across home, workplace, and public locations. In contrast to earlier studies that treat charging location as a one-time, discrete choice, we examine preferences for combinations of all three locations over a monthly period. We employ a multiple discrete–continuous extreme value (MDCEV) model using stated preference data from 881 employed EV drivers across the United States. Results show that 88.9% of charging decisions involve multiple locations. Home charging is preferred overall, followed by workplace and public. Drivers with private driveways, single-family homes, or solar panels, as well as older adults have higher home charging preferences, though battery storage moderates the pull of solar toward home. Urban residents rely more on public charging, while workplace charging is highly price-elastic, offering employers a demand management lever. Our study underscores the importance of examining charging behavior as a portfolio allocation decision.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Renewable energy investment and grid connection strategy for competitive carbon-free ports
Authors: Guotao Zhang, Qi Zhang, Yong Zhou, Xiao Yang, Qianli Ma
Abstract: Renewable energy investment has become an effective and feasible pathway for ports to achieve zero carbon emissions. However, considering the power demand of ports and the characteristics of renewable energy and the electricity grid, deciding the level of renewable energy investment and the grid connection strategy remains a critical issue. Therefore, we propose a multi-stage game-theoretical model to analyze decision-making processes related to renewable energy investment in the context of inter-port competition. The equilibrium results reveal that low electricity costs incentivize competing ports to increase renewable energy investments through grid connection, paradoxically creating a Prisoner’s Dilemma where decarbonization progresses at the expense of port profit. A government subsidy scheme is proposed to enable a Profit-Environment win–win situation by aligning port incentives with emissions targets. Two case studies of Tianjin–Qingdao Ports and Shanghai–Ningbo-Zhoushan Ports support the findings and show different economic and environmental implications across port settings.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Mode choice shifts to electric micromobility for car and public transport users
Authors: Yikang Wu, Mehmet Yildirimoglu, Zuduo Zheng
Abstract: Electric micro-mobility (EMM) is increasingly recognised as a sustainable travel option, yet mode choice preferences for EMM relative to conventional modes remain insufficiently understood. This study advances current knowledge by jointly examining standalone personal micro-mobility and multimodal public transport (PT)-integrated shared micromobility mode choice behaviour. An online stated-preference survey of 1671 Brisbane residents yielded 9858 choice observations from car and public transport users. The experimental design incorporates contextual conditions (e.g., weather, distance) and trip attributes (e.g., travel time, cost, waiting, congestion, and bikeway quality) to improve behavioural realism. Latent Class Choice Models reveal substantial heterogeneity: although a resistant segment is present, most respondents show willingness to switch to EMM under favourable conditions. Spatial and class-profile analyses further indicate that EMM-leaning segments are more likely to be male, under 49, full-time employed, higher-income, highly educated, and living in more central areas.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Do electric vehicles reduce transit use? Environmental-behavioral insights from causal machine learning
Authors: Shuo Yang, Leyu Zhou, Junren Wang, Liang Guo, Xiaoli Sun, Frank Witlox
Abstract: Although electric vehicles (EVs) provide environmental benefits, their impacts on travel behavior, specifically transit choice, remain underexplored. Empirical evidence on how the built environment and EV ownership jointly influence transit choice is, to our knowledge, scarce. This study addresses gaps by applying double machine learning to a large-scale household travel survey from Wuhan, China, in 2020. The approach simultaneously addresses nonlinear effects and the endogeneity of vehicle ownership when examining relationships among the built environment, vehicle ownership, and transit choice. The results show that EV ownership reduces the probability of using transit more than conventional vehicles, about 26% versus 16%. For EV users, built environment attributes gain predictive importance, yet many exert weaker or opposite effects on transit choice, suggesting possible failure of conventional transit-supportive interventions. Using causal machine learning, these findings provide new evidence for revisiting the behavioral foundations of transit-oriented development in the context of transportation electrification.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Consumer preferences and diffusion potential of integrating autonomous and electric vehicle technologies
Authors: Yerim Rieu, Jihye Choi, Kyungah Kim
Abstract: Electric vehicles (EVs) and autonomous vehicles (AVs) technologies are increasingly promoted together as a strategy for achieving carbon neutrality, yet consumer perceptions of this convergence remain underexplored. This study examines preferences for autonomous electric vehicles (AEVs) using a discrete choice experiment and mixed logit analysis of Korean consumers. Results show that, for EVs, a one-level increase in automation generates a willingness-to-pay (WTP) more than three times higher than for other fuel types, suggesting that integrating the two technologies can reduce reluctance toward EV adoption. Scenario analysis further indicates that while automation modestly raises the probability of EV choice, the effect is more sensitive to costs than to technology levels. When AV usage fees exceed consumer WTP, the diffusion effect is limited. These findings highlight that integrating EV and AV technologies can strengthen EV competitiveness and support greenhouse gas reduction, but that pricing and incentive design remain critical.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Unraveling the impacts of heavy rainfall on cross-city human mobility
Authors: Huan Liu, Yoshio Kajitani, Yongsheng Yang, Kyo Yamaguchi, Hirokazu Tatano
Abstract: Heavy rainfall frequently disrupts transportation networks and further interrupts human mobility. The collectively impact of disasters on human mobility has been explored, but few empirical studies have decoupled the impact patterns of disasters on cross-city mobility and their interplays with transportation disruptions. Therefore, this study integrated large-scale point-type origin-destination mobility data (66,874,859 records) with other multi-source data to reveal the impact of the 2018 Heavy Rain event in Japan on travel patterns across cities and purpose-specific travel activities. Results reveal that mobility changepoints strongly synchronized with the disruption, restoration, and reopening of transportation networks, and alternative routes play a decisive role in speeding regional mobility recovery. Moreover, essential activities were far less interrupted by heavy rainfall than non-essential activities, while peak daily commuting decreased by 8%, and peak daily shopping trips dropped by 20%. These findings offer empirical evidence on prioritizing critical links, redundancy planning, and emergency response.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Multimodality and subjective wellbeing: evidence, insights, and research frontiers
Authors: Xingxing Fu, Dea van Lierop, Dick Ettema
Abstract: Multimodal travel is increasingly promoted as a strategy to enhance environmental sustainability. Meanwhile, transport policies also target social sustainability, it is thus essential to understand how multimodal travel influences people’s subjective wellbeing (SWB). This literature review synthesises existing research evidence and uncovers potential pathways linking multimodality to SWB. The review considers multimodality as using multiple transport modes within a single trip (i.e., trip-level multimodality) and over an extended period (i.e., individual-level multimodality). Individual-level multimodality influences SWB by facilitating activity participation across various destinations and diversifying activities during travel, while also potentially increasing daily travel expenses and exposure to uncertainty and unsafe conditions. Trip-level multimodality affects SWB through heightened experiential disutility and coordination complexity associated with intermodal transfers, as well as intensified exposure to external environments during non-primary trip legs (e.g. access and egress legs). This review develops a conceptual framework and a research agenda to address key gaps, supporting the development of multimodal policies that advance both social and environmental sustainability.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Bus transit to wellbeing: active aging pathways in China’s most aged megacity
Authors: Wanting Liu, Jie Yu, Jing Zhao, Xiaofei Liu
Abstract: This study examines how specific components of bus transit service influence older adults’ life satisfaction and self-rated health through the mediating role of active aging. Using survey data from 709 older adults and interviews with 25 participants collected between 2024 and 2025 in Shanghai, China’s most aged megacity, we integrate structural equation modeling with large language model–assisted qualitative analysis. Transit service is disaggregated into bus stop infrastructure, on-board features, and driver service experience. Results show that driver service has a strong positive effect on active aging, which in turn enhances both health and life satisfaction, whereas infrastructure-related features exhibit weak or negative indirect effects. Qualitative findings indicate that unmet assistance needs, unreliable information, and inconsistent use of accessibility features undermine the psychological benefits of physical improvements, while attentive driver behavior strengthens confidence and autonomy. These findings highlight the importance of human-centered service in translating infrastructure investment into well-being gains.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Co-adoption of solar panels and electric vehicles: Evidence from California
Authors: Sachin B. Badole, Jeremy Firestone, Martin D. Heintzelman, George Parsons
Abstract: This study examines consumer preferences for co-adoption of residential rooftop solar photovoltaic (RPV) systems and electric vehicles (EVs) in California, including factors that influence consumer adoption decisions. Using a contingent-behavior experiment with 1,311 California households, grouped by prior technology adoption ownership. Respondents evaluated hypothetical EVs or RPVs contracts, depending on their adoption status. A fractional logistic regression model was applied to assess co-adoption decisions. Results show that EV owners are more likely to adopt RPV systems, and RPV owners are more likely to adopt EVs. RPV or EV adoption is more likely among wealthier, male, liberals, larger, and Democratic households, with EV adoption also among younger, Asian, and medium-income respondents. EV adoption preference declines as costs increase (similar for RPVs), charging time increases, and driving range decreases. These results clarify households’ preferences and the factors driving co-adoption, providing guidance for policies aimed at reducing carbon emissions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Contextualizing asymmetric drivers of older passengers’ satisfaction with rapid transit: A mixed-methods approach
Authors: Haosen Yang, Zhihong Yao, Giancarlos Parady, Linchuan Yang, Jason Cao
Abstract: Population aging is reshaping transit demand, yet transit service design often remains based on average-passenger perspectives that overlook older passengers’ needs. Moreover, there is limited evidence on the nonlinear effects of service attributes on transit satisfaction; existing research is predominantly quantitative, with little qualitative context. To address these gaps, this study investigates older passengers’ satisfaction with metro and BRT services in Chengdu (China) using a mixed-methods approach. Drawing on survey data from 928 older passengers, which yielded 1,068 mode-specific observations, we integrated gradient boosting decision tree models with impact-asymmetry analysis to identify key drivers of overall satisfaction and their asymmetric effects. We further interviewed 30 older passengers to contextualize the observed asymmetric patterns. The results show that most service attributes exert nonlinear and asymmetric effects on overall satisfaction, with key attributes varying across transit modes. For metro service, ease of transfer, information at stops, and transfer time require priority attention; for BRT, seat availability, waiting time, and transfer time are most critical. Overall, this study demonstrates the value of combining nonlinear modeling with qualitative evidence to better understand older passengers’ satisfaction and to inform targeted, age-friendly transit improvements.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Integrated optimization of facility location and routing for timely emergency disaster response
Authors: Joonghoo Park, San Kwon, Hyungjoo Cha, Meng Xu, Taesu Cheong
Abstract: We develop a novel decision-support model for disaster response operations, the Temporary Medical Center (TMC) Location-Routing Problem with Manpower Allocation (TMCLRPwMA), which integrates decisions regarding and jointly optimizes the placement of TMCs, ambulance routing, and healthcare staff allocation under a limited relief budget. To address the problem’s NP-hard nature, we propose a novel metaheuristic method, the Hybrid Genetic Algorithm Plus (HGA+). The proposed mixed-integer linear programming formulation and HGA+ are evaluated across multiple synthetic and real-world instances. Numerical experiments demonstrate that HGA+ consistently achieves near-optimal solutions with superior computational performance relative to exact methods. Sensitivity analyses assess the impact of staffing and budget variations. Finally, we conduct a case study calibrated to Seoul’s emergency medical system to demonstrate the model’s real-world applicability. The results show that our framework can reduce maximum rescue times and improve equity in patient access compared to a policy-based simulator that replicates current dispatch rules.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: From policy to practice: accessibility impacts of Wrocław’s proposed low-emission zone
Authors: Marta Borowska-Stefańska, Maxim A. Dulebenets, Mariusz Lamprecht, Tadeusz Pupar, Alireza Sahebgharani, Szymon Wiśniewski
Abstract: Low Emission Zones (LEZs) are a flagship climate-air policy in European transport, yet evidence on how design choices redistribute congestion and accessibility is limited. We evaluate nine proposed LEZ variants for Wrocław (Poland) for 2025, combining three spatial extents with three compliance stringency levels. Using the city’s official PTV Visum macromodel, each variant is implemented by scaling within-zone link capacities to reflect the share of compliant vehicles and re-running assignment to derive peak-hour flows, speeds, and travel-time skims. We then quantify short-trip potential accessibility (population-weighted, exponential decay) and classify transport zones by sensitivity using k-means on changes in travel time to the city centre. Results reveal a strongly design-dependent relation between environmental ambition and network performance, with pronounced spatial heterogeneity, providing a policy-ready, transferable framework for LEZ design and phasing.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Tiered standards, differential effects: a quasi-experimental study of China’s vehicle emission policies
Authors: Chao Wang, Jing Xue, Hongyi Xie, Fred Phillips, Gang Liu, Fan Zhang
Abstract: Building a sustainable transport system requires effective control of vehicle emissions, a key challenge in pollution and carbon reduction. This paper employs a Difference-in-Differences (DID) model to evaluate the effects of China’s upgraded vehicle emission standards (China IV and V) on CO, HC, and NOx reductions. Heterogeneity effects across vehicle types (diesel/gasoline, light-duty/heavy-duty) are further examined. Key findings: (1) Emission standards significantly reduce total vehicle emissions; (2) Diesel vehicles show greater responsiveness than gasoline vehicles, with distinct policy focuses for light-duty compared with heavy-duty types; (3) China IV exhibits a tiered reduction pattern of HC > NO x > CO, while China V shows HC > CO > NO x ; (4) Light-duty vehicles outperform heavy-duty vehicles across all emissions, with diesel vehicles demonstrating stronger CO and HC mitigation than gasoline counterparts. These findings offer actionable insights for refining tiered emission regulations and advancing the low-carbon transition in China’s transportation sector.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Data-driven analysis of EV public charging station demand across heterogeneous built environment
Authors: Junfang Tian, Shuo Li, Kun Wang, Zhenjie Zheng, Qianran Zhang
Abstract: Public charging stations (PCS) have become critical infrastructure in urban transportation systems. PCS charging demand patterns are driven by complex mechanisms that conventional methods struggle to quantify, while the influence of the built environment (BE) remains underexplored. An integrated empirical framework is proposed that combines machine learning and causal inference models to analyze PCS demand patterns and generate evidence-based policy implications. Specifically, XGBoost with partial dependence plots is employed to predict demand, identify key determinants, and reveal nonlinear relationships, followed by double machine learning to quantify the causal effects of critical policy-relevant factors. We construct a real-world charging dataset incorporating BE, temporal, and price attributes for empirical analysis. Results show that charging demand is shaped by public transport accessibility and the spatial configuration of PCS. Electricity price has a stronger negative impact in areas farther away from subway stations. These findings support optimized charging infrastructure planning and targeted policy interventions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Wildfire evacuation analysis using facebook data: Evidence from Palisades and Eaton fires
Authors: Shangkun Jiang, Ruggiero Lovreglio, Thomas J. Cova, Sangung Park, Susu Xu, Xilei Zhao
Abstract: The growing frequency and intensity of wildfires pose serious threats to communities in wildland-urban interface regions. Understanding evacuation behavior is critical for effective emergency planning. This study analyzes evacuation during the 2025 Palisades and Eaton Fires using high-resolution Facebook data. We propose a comprehensive framework to derive wildfire evacuation-related metrics, including compliance rate, departure timing, delay, origin-destination flows, travel distance, and destination types. A new metric, Damage-Evacuation Disparity Index (DEDI), identifies areas with severe structural damage but low evacuation compliance. Results reveal spatiotemporal heterogeneity: residents closer to the fire evacuated earlier, whereas late or nighttime orders led to lower compliance and longer delays. Contrasting patterns between East and West Altadena further illustrate this disparity. DEDI-identified communities exhibited higher social vulnerability and fire risk. Most evacuations concluded in residential areas, while longer trips concentrated in hotels and public facilities. These findings showcase the Facebook data's potential for data-driven wildfire evacuation planning.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Curbing the car or charging at the curb?
Authors: Adam Millard-Ball, Jasmine Law
Abstract: Do electric vehicles (EVs), and the expansion of curbside charging infrastructure in particular, undermine efforts to reduce vehicle travel? As EVs gain market share, decisionmakers may be less inclined to support policies such as bicycle lanes and reduced parking if they compete for space with EV chargers. We find no evidence, however, of policy substitution. Surveys in Los Angeles indicate that public support for policies to reduce driving is not swayed by the availability of EV charging. Furthermore, interviews in North American cities reveal that local officials are cautious about locking in scarce curbspace for EVs, and universally prioritized curb uses such as bicycle and bus lanes, street trees, and parklets. In our sample of early adopter cities, EV charging is not currently diminishing the political will for policies to reduce driving. However, this caution has slowed the rollout of curbside charging in North America.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Integrated optimization of mobile battery swapping and charging systems under uncertainty
Authors: Yong Zhang, Xiaohan Yin, Ming Cheng, Weike Lu, Xiangwang Hu, Xiang Peng
Abstract: This paper proposes an integrated optimization framework for designing mobile battery swapping and charging service systems (MBSCSs). These systems use battery-swapping vans (BSVs) to deliver charged batteries to electric vehicles (EVs) and perform on-site swaps. BSVs then return to dedicated charging stations to reload with charged batteries, forming a closed-loop service. Mismatches and uncertainties in demand, service, and charging can disrupt this loop. To address this, we develop a three-level stochastic optimization framework to jointly determine the numbers and allocation of BSVs, charging racks, and batteries. The top level determines the overall system scale, the middle allocates BSVs to jurisdictions to minimize expected response time, and the bottom allocates batteries and racks to minimize charging queues. Customized heuristic algorithms solve the model efficiently. Metrics are introduced to evaluate MBSCS performance. Validated through two case studies, the framework demonstrates improved service performance and scalability.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Comparative evaluation of fume suppressants for reducing hazardous emissions from asphalt binder: Mechanisms, efficiency, and rheological performance
Authors: Feng Ma, Jinshuo Yan, Ke Shi, Zhen Fu, Xinye Jiang, Ruizhe Huang, Shuo Wan, Tianyi Zhang
Abstract: Suppressing hazardous fume emissions from asphalt binders during high-temperature processing is essential for protecting occupational health and advancing green pavement construction. This study systematically compared three representative fume suppressants with distinct action mechanisms, namely melamine (MEL, chemical inhibition), aluminum trihydrate (ATH, flame-retardant), and ZSM-5 zeolite (ZEO, physical adsorption). A custom-built sealed fume detection system was employed to quantify the suppression efficiencies for VOCs, CO, H 2 S, and SO 2 at 140, 160, and 180 °C. The Michaelis–Menten equation was applied to fit dose–response curves, enabling unified cross-suppressant comparison. Temperature sweep, frequency sweep, and bending beam rheometer (BBR) tests were performed to evaluate the high- and low-temperature rheological properties, while Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) were conducted to elucidate the physicochemical mechanisms. The three suppressants exhibited clearly differentiated emission-control behaviors governed by their mechanisms. The binder modified with 7% ZEO delivered the highest and most temperature-stable overall suppression, sustaining VOC reduction at 57.5%–59.9% across 140–180 °C and remaining the most effective against acidic gases through microporous adsorption, with H 2 S and SO 2 suppression reaching 73.2% and 68.1% at 180 °C. MEL displayed a pronounced low-dosage threshold effect, with the binder modified with 2% MEL attaining 62.5% VOC suppression at 140 °C and 57.4% CO suppression at 180 °C while higher dosage yielded no further gain. ATH suppression increased monotonically with temperature, yet remained the lowest of the three across the tested range. Rheologically, all three suppressants improved high-temperature rutting resistance, with the binder modified with 2% MEL raising the rutting factor by 92.8% at 64 °C. At low temperature, ATH raised system rigidity and compromised flexibility, whereas ZEO-modified binders offered the most favorable stress relaxation capacity and the lowest glass transition temperature of −18.06 °C. FTIR and TGA confirmed that all three suppressants were physically dispersed in the asphalt matrix without chemical interaction, functioning respectively through gas-phase dilution, endothermic dehydration, and microporous adsorption. These findings provide a mechanistic and performance-based reference for selecting fume suppressants that balance emission reduction and rheological compatibility in asphalt binder applications.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Decadal Evolution, spatial Heterogeneity, and drivers of China’s highway vehicle emissions
Authors: Xiaomeng Wu, Youchao Wang, Yifan Wen, Daoyuan Yang, Rui Wu, Shaojun Zhang, Ye Wu
Abstract: Intercity transportation reflects complex socioeconomic dynamics, yet few studies have assessed long-term national emission patterns. Using 2010–2024 traffic data, we develop a machine learning-based predictor (C-Flow) to map link-level emissions across China’s intercity highways. CO 2 emissions show strong urban agglomeration effects, while NO X is concentrated along major freight corridors. Significant mismatches between vehicle registration and operation reveal that highways contribute 79 % of national heavy-duty truck (HDT) emissions, and registration-based inventories can underestimate emissions by up to 100 % in freight-intensive provinces. From 2010 to 2024, highway THC, NO X , and PM 2.5 declined by 39 %, 14 %, and 67 %, respectively, but CO 2 rose by 166 %. Since 2018, only two provinces have achieved simultaneous CO 2 reductions, highlighting persistent mitigation challenges driven by economic growth, freight demand, and limited efficiency gains. While end-of-pipe controls remain vital, demand-side measures, such as reducing transport intensity, improving freight efficiency, and optimizing transport structures, are essential for long-term co-mitigation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Does the mobility-as-a-service platform alleviate traffic congestion in China?
Authors: Zhao Liu, Rong Song, Bin Su, Chen Li
Abstract: Traditional traffic management is increasingly constrained by land scarcity and rising costs. As a digital governance tool, Mobility-as-a-Service (MaaS) integrates diverse transport modes to improve travel efficiency. However, most studies have focused on individual MaaS components such as public transport and bike-sharing, with limited evidence on the congestion-alleviating effect of MaaS as an integrated platform. This study examines the congestion-alleviating effect of the Beijing MaaS platform using the augmented synthetic control method. The results show that the platform significantly alleviates traffic congestion, with stronger effects on working days than on non-working days. While the platform reduces the number of mild congestion days, its effect on the number of high congestion days is not statistically significant. These results suggest that MaaS can serve as a flexible instrument of urban mobility governance for easing routine congestion, although its effectiveness remains context dependent and ultimately constrained by transport system capacity.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Enhancing resilience of urban cold chain logistics: A predict-and-prescribe approach
Authors: Xinyi Fang, Linjun Lu, Poly Z.H. Sun
Abstract: To evaluate resilience strategies for food cold chains facing climate-intensified floods, we develop a predict-and-prescribe approach that integrates vulnerability prediction with policy simulation. The predictive component utilizes a probabilistic vulnerability graph attention network to rank facility vulnerability, outperforming benchmarks by 33.4% in accuracy. The prescription embeds these rankings within a flood-coupled cold chain agent-based model to simulate thermodynamic spoilage driven by flood-induced operational failures.Across flood intensities, prescription reveals an objective mismatch: protecting structurally central nodes yields 15% higher system benefit than targeting predicted high-loss sites. This gap is driven by an ‘inventory bomb’, in which 90.8% of losses concentrate at downstream retail nodes. In response, we identify a ‘layered defense’ hybrid strategy combining physical robustness, resource redundancy, and network flexibility as optimal.These findings establish a dual-tool policy framework: use AI for ex-ante risk provisioning, but prioritize structural leverage over predicted loss magnitude for emergency triage in catastrophic events.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Penny wise, emission foolish? Quantifying the economic and environmental trade-offs of fuel tankering strategy
Authors: Shuai Yue, Qing Ji, Chunan Wang, Changmin Jiang, Anming Zhang
Abstract: Fuel tankering strategy (FTS) allows airlines to reduce costs by carrying extra fuel, creating an economic and environmental trade-off. This paper evaluates this behavior using more than 27 million flight records and jet fuel prices from the Asian market between 2019 and 2023. Using high dimensional fixed effects models and propensity score matching, we find that a USD 100 per ton increase in the fuel price gap between Mainland China and Hong Kong is associated with 192.2 kg higher carbon emissions per flight and 16.30 additional monthly flights. Over 58 months, fuel cost savings of USD 83.90 million far exceed the USD 3.38 million in social carbon costs, creating a net welfare gain of USD 80.52 million. Heterogeneity analysis shows positive emission responses of 72.41 kg for Japan, 148.4 kg for South Korea, and 422.3 kg for Singapore. Policymakers should resolve fuel price distortions rather than relying solely on environmental regulations.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Arctic shipping route design with CO2-black carbon trade-offs
Authors: Dung-Ying Lin
Abstract: Arctic shipping growth along the Northern Sea Route raises pressing environmental concerns, particularly regarding black carbon (BC), a short-lived climate forcer rarely modeled as a distinct routing objective. This paper develops a two-stage stochastic multi-objective optimization model that simultaneously minimizes expected cost, CO 2 , and BC emissions under sea ice uncertainty, with strategic deployment fixed before uncertainty realization and operational decisions adjusted afterward. A Criterion-Space Benders Decomposition (CSBD) algorithm reuses optimality cuts across Pareto frontier regions and solves bounded scalarized subproblems to proven optimality within prescribed MIP tolerances. Experiments on 16 synthetic and three AIS-informed instances confirm that CO 2 alone is an inadequate proxy for BC: bi-objective models produce 20 to 128% more BC at matched cost or CO 2 levels. Between 56.5% and 84.6% of BC can be reduced through operating plan selection without route redesign, though near-complete elimination requires cost premiums up to 500%, highlighting the practical value of explicit BC-cost trade-off analysis for Arctic emission governance.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Multi-agent deep reinforcement learning with cross efficiency social rewards for unmanned aerial vehicle collaborative optimization in ship emission monitoring
Authors: Weipan Zhang, Jihong Chen, Kui Yi, Li Dong, Xianhua Wu
Abstract: Ship emissions constitute a major source of air pollution in coastal regions. To address the challenges associated with high-precision and dynamic emission monitoring, this paper proposes a cooperative unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) monitoring framework that integrates data envelopment analysis (DEA) with multi-agent reinforcement learning. Specifically, a path planning and sampling decision-making model based on multi-agent proximal policy optimization (MAPPO) is developed, and a DEA-based cross efficiency social reward (CESR) mechanism is introduced to characterize the relative efficiency and cooperative relationships among UAVs under multiple objectives, including energy consumption, spatial coverage, and emission inversion performance. This mechanism guides UAVs to form an appropriate division of labor in dynamic, multi-source, and uncertain environments, thereby reducing redundant sampling and improving overall monitoring efficiency. Furthermore, a unified simulation environment is established by coupling a pollution plume dispersion model driven by realistic wind fields, a ship emission inversion model, and UAV dynamics and energy consumption constraints. Based on real automatic identification system (AIS) ship trajectories and ERA5 wind field data from the offshore area of the Copenhagen Port, Denmark, systematic comparative experiments are conducted under scenarios with varying ship densities and wind field complexities. The results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves significant improvements in emission inversion accuracy, detection capability, energy efficiency, and cooperative stability. In particular, it exhibits stronger robustness under conditions of high ship density and intense wind field disturbances. These findings provide a new cooperative decision-making paradigm for multi-UAV ship emission monitoring that combines performance enhancement with improved interpretability.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Environmental impact analysis of shared autonomous vehicles: A comprehensive review
Authors: Lin Tu, Min Xu, W.Y. Szeto
Abstract: Shared autonomous vehicles (SAVs) have the potential to address the environmental challenges faced by traditional transportation systems. However, the overall environmental impacts of SAVs remain underexplored. This article systematically reviews studies published between 2014 and 2025, examining the environmental impacts of SAVs across five key aspects: air pollution, land use and pollution, the greenhouse effect, noise pollution, and water pollution. Furthermore, it identifies research gaps and proposes future research directions from five perspectives: travel behavior, service operational modes, emerging technologies, policy dynamics, and research methodologies. Overall, this article provides a comprehensive review of studies on the environmental impacts of SAVs, and outlines a roadmap for future investigations.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Agent-based modeling of resilience and cascading failures in highway charging networks
Authors: Jian Yuan, Qijian Zhao, Qing Yu, Haoran Jiang, Weiyao Yang, Haoran Zhang
Abstract: The proliferation of electric vehicles demands resilient highway charging networks, yet existing models often overlook the coupling of microscopic driver behavior with macroscopic congestion. To address this, we propose a data-driven, agent-based modeling framework for resilience assessment. Applied to the Yangtze River Delta network, the model utilizes novel metrics to identify emergent saturation phenomena and phase transitions, including Selective Filtering and Capacity-Performance Discrepancy. We categorize station resilience into four distinct patterns: High-Sensitivity, Oversaturation, Graceful Degradation, and Robust-Brittle. Crucially, the study decodes the physical mechanisms driving these patterns, distinguishing between pseudo-recovery driven by service denial and true service degradation. Furthermore, the analysis reveals how mandatory charging needs trigger cascading failures, propagating pressure along main corridors to create secondary failure hubs. These findings provide quantitative support for targeted network optimization and emergency management.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Corrigendum to “Emission reduction in shipping supply chain: Game-theoretic analysis of shippers’ dual preferences” [Transp. Res. Part D: Transp. Environ. 155 (2026) 105341]
Authors: Yuan Zhao, Xuanxuan Sheng, Dan Wang

Title: Infrastructure access and routines shape heterogeneous public EV charging preferences
Authors: Hossein Gazmeh, Omar Faruqe Hamim, Torsten Reimer, Juan Pablo Loaiza-Ramírez, Satish V. Ukkusuri, Xinwu Qian
Abstract: Existing research models EV charging choice as tradeoffs among station attributes, obscuring qualitatively distinct behavioral profiles that govern how tradeoffs are formed. Using survey data from 365 BEV owners, we combine factor analysis, latent profile analysis, and inverse propensity weighting (IPW) to identify preference dimensions, segment users, and estimate causal drivers of profile membership. Factor analysis reveals eight latent dimensions spanning station-facing choice attributes and user-facing contextual factors. Latent profile analysis identifies two groups: Efficiency-Oriented Users (76%), prioritizing accessibility and cost, and Information-Responsive Users (24%), emphasizing provider trust, amenities, and situational compatibility. IPW estimates show that private charger access (OR = 2.39), business use (OR = 2.70), and public charging frequency (weekly OR = 7.43) increase Information-Responsive membership, while commuting use decreases it (OR = 0.47). These results demonstrate that preference heterogeneity is shaped by infrastructural access and behavioral routines, offering a preference-based explanation for station underutilization and underscoring the need for differentiated infrastructure planning.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Two-stage fleet size and mix electric vehicle routing problem with energy estimation
Authors: Raphael Andreolli, Mikael Nybacka, Erik Jenelius, Ciarán J. O’Reilly, Martin Hede
Abstract: Decarbonization of road transportation in Europe is slow, while interest in emerging technologies and operating strategies with environmental and operational benefits is increasing.To assess their impacts, vehicle routing models support strategic fleet assessment, yet many rely on simplified energy models and neglect key vehicle- and system-level factors, limiting evaluation of technologies and operating strategies.We develop a two-stage optimization framework that determines fleet size, mix, and routes for simultaneous pickup and delivery, estimating realistic energy use on road networks. The energy model is evaluated against electric-truck data, and the framework quantifies trade-offs among driverless multipurpose, human-driven combustion, and battery-electric fleets in combined heavy-goods freight-and-waste city logistics.Although the energy model overestimates absolute energy use, it reproduces the main subroute ranking and captures fleet- and network-specific effects. The framework supports energy-informed strategic, tactical, and operational decisions; key limitations are scalability and that results reflect automation rather than full multipurpose capability.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Lower volatility, lower profit? Smart trap in two-dimensional port competition
Authors: Baozhuang Niu, Jiayun Liu, Yiyuan Ruan, Mingming Leng
Abstract: Ports face growing demand volatility and congestion, threatening operational efficiency and environmental performance. AI-powered smart port technologies promise to mitigate these challenges by making congestion information visible to port users. However, this paper shows that such visibility does not always deliver the expected benefits when ports compete on both price and congestion situations. Providing more congestion information may paradoxically amplify demand fluctuations and worsen congestion, a phenomenon we term the “smart trap.” We further show that the value of developing smart port depends critically on port capacity levels and their demand correlation. When port capacity is tight and demand is moderately correlated, developing smart port can increase congestion and emissions. Our analysis cautions that digitalization does not universally improve port sustainability, and this finding is verified by an empirical study using Hamburg and Bremerhaven port data.

Title: Cost-competitiveness of battery electric vehicles and two-wheelers: Evidence from Indonesia
Authors: Rio Pradana Manggala Putra, Zsuzsanna Csereklyei, Lasantha Meegahapola
Abstract: This study investigates the current and projected cost-competitiveness of battery electric vehicles (BEVs) and electric two-wheelers (E2Ws) against conventional internal combustion engine (ICE) counterparts in the Indonesian market by examining their total cost of ownership (TCO). We find that existing policies have made BEVs and E2Ws purchased in 2024 already more cost-competitive than ICE vehicles and two-wheelers across all categories. However, in the absence of current tax concessions and subsidies, long-range E2Ws would not achieve cost-competitiveness over their internal combustion counterparts until 2027. The TCO of electric vehicles is also sensitive to battery-pack cost and cost projections as well as to the annual distance travelled. Despite their cost-competitiveness, the uptake of BEVs and E2Ws is still limited in Indonesia. Policy action may be focused on establishing the necessary support infrastructure to enable uptake.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Evolution of electric bus systems: A review of models, methods, and future directions
Authors: Di Huang, Feng Li, Jie Yin, Yu Zhou, Yiming Bie, Hua Wang, Zhiyuan Liu
Abstract: Electric buses (EBs) are important to the transition toward low-carbon and environmentally sustainable urban mobility. In this paper, we consolidate EB-related studies through a qualitative synthesis and a bibliometric analysis of recent publications. The bibliometric results track the field’s growth, identify influential countries and institutions, and reveal major thematic clusters. The qualitative review examines central topics, including battery performance and degradation, charging facility planning and shared charging strategies, operational optimization, and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) interaction and implementation considerations. The findings highlight persistent gaps, including limited consideration of battery aging, stakeholder-oriented value sharing, and practical power-grid participation, indicating opportunities for more robust and implementable EB planning and operation frameworks. This study offers an integrated perspective to support methodological development and practical EB system implementation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Supply-demand and income-integrated perspectives of healthcare accessibility in high-density, transit-oriented cities
Authors: Zijin Zhou, Esther H.K. Yung, Shuai Yuan, Lingfang Shao, Xiqian Zhang
Abstract: Despite Hong Kong’s high-density, transit-oriented setting, healthcare-seeking travel burdens are disproportionate for low-income residents and accumulate with recurrent visits. This study addresses the limitations of traditional supply–demand-based healthcare accessibility by combining the Gaussian three-step floating catchment area method with an income-integrated accessibility measure that captures income-heterogeneous travel burdens. This framework addresses two questions: where integrated accessibility outcomes converge or diverge, and how transport-related built environment and socio-economic characteristics correlate with these patterns. The main findings are: (i) convergence clusters in the urban core and rural areas, whereas divergence concentrates in low-income, inner-city areas, affluent urban fringe, and well-connected new towns; (ii) MNL analyses show convergence arises where healthcare supply, transit connectivity, and income reinforce each other, while divergence arises where service distribution is misaligned with transport-related built environment and income levels. These findings demonstrate that healthcare planning should coordinate facility distribution with income-sensitive transport policies to address the accessibility mismatch.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Are sustainability priorities aligned across supply chain stakeholders in Europe?
Authors: Daniela Castaño-Herrera, Natalia Sobrino, Jose Manuel Vassallo
Abstract: The logistics sector involves multiple stakeholders whose roles, incentives, and responsibilities shape how sustainability goals are prioritised. Yet empirical evidence on whether these priorities align across supply chain actors remains limited, particularly in Europe. This study investigates differences in sustainability priorities across stakeholder roles and examines the perceived importance and progress of key green logistics drivers using a Europe-wide survey and a multi-method approach combining the Analytic Hierarchy Process and comparative statistical analyses. Results show that priorities are largely aligned across European regions, but significant differences emerge across stakeholder groups. Academics and infrastructure managers emphasise environmental goals, cargo owners and operators prioritise economic and social aspects, and public authorities give greater weight to governance. Technology-based innovations are perceived as more promising drivers than collaborative and other non-technological mechanisms, although their implementation progress remains moderate. These findings support the design of more integrated and coordinated sustainability strategies across Europe’s logistics ecosystem.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Electric or fuel? Green routing optimization with time uncertainty in fourth-party logistics
Authors: Hongliang Xu, Min Huang, Songchen Jiang, Yuxin Zhang, Junwei Wang, Xingwei Wang
Abstract: This paper investigates a green fourth-party logistics (4PL) routing optimization problem, incorporating transportation time uncertainty and the strategic choice between fuel vehicles (FVs) and electric vehicles (EVs) to reduce carbon emissions. To ensure timely delivery under time uncertainty, a mixed-integer chance-constrained programming (MICCP) model is developed. Given limited historical data, the MICCP model is reformulated through sample average approximation method and a Sample Mean-based Heuristic (SMH) algorithm is further proposed, which works as a data-driven method for potentially broader chance constrained programming with left-hand uncertainty. Numerical study validates the effectiveness of proposed models and algorithm, and offers managerial insights on balancing electric and fuel vehicle usage. We find that (1) stricter carbon tax policies do not necessarily motivate 4PLs to adopt EVs for emission reduction; (2) increasing switching time between transport providers will weaken the pooling advantages of 4PL mode, but encouraging the adoption of EVs.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Transit users’ preferences for street infrastructure during daytime and night-time walking
Authors: Rong Liu, Paulina Maria Neisch
Abstract: Understanding how street infrastructure influences route choices during access and egress walking trips is essential to promoting pedestrian-oriented environments around urban rail transit (URT) stations and extending their catchment areas. This study employed a visual route-choice experiment with 651 transit users in Guiyang, China, using a mixed logit model (MXL) incorporating interactions between individual characteristics and route attributes to evaluate preferences for street infrastructure during daytime and night-time walking. Results indicate that pedestrians favor routes to metro stations with narrower driveways, wider pavements, and tree- or hedge-lined walkways in the daytime. Adequate lighting and improved natural and mechanical surveillance effectively mitigate night-time security concerns. Preference heterogeneity was further observed across gender, age, and primary travel mode. The visualized experiment provides empirical evidence for designing pedestrian-friendly streets that enhance walking comfort and safety, thereby supporting sustainable transit use.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: From performance to environmental benefits: recycling solid waste for low-carbon pavements
Authors: Jiaqiu Xu, Shaowei Zhang, Zhaojie Chen, Xinghao Feng, Fuliao Zou, Zhen Leng
Abstract: Recycling solid waste as fillers in asphalt mixtures offers a sustainable approach for low-carbon pavements. This study evaluated five common solid wastes as mineral filler alternatives through integrated performance, environmental safety, and life cycle assessments (LCA). Results showed that steel slag (SS), iron tailings (IT), and waste cement (CE) fillers notably enhanced rutting, moisture, and fatigue resistance, with SS exhibiting 20% lower fracture energy than limestone filler in low-temperature cracking. Leaching tests confirmed heavy metal levels were well below regulatory limits, indicating minimal environmental risk. In a Guangdong highway case, SS, CE, and IT fillers reduced rehabilitation interventions from five to three over 40 years, while desulfurization gypsum (DG) reduced them to four. LCA revealed SS, IT, and CE fillers decreased all environmental impact categories by over 32%, with CE achieving the greatest reductions in human health, ecosystem, and resource impacts. This framework supports sustainable pavement engineering using solid waste.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Nonlinear built environment impacts on travel behavior: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Authors: Chun Yin, Senqi Tian, Tao Tao
Abstract: Built environment improvements are widely recognized as essential for reducing automobile dependence and promoting active travel and transit use. A growing body of empirical evidence indicates that the built environment exerts nonlinear impacts on travel behavior. This study reviews existing research focused on these nonlinear associations. Utilizing a novel data extraction and aggregation process, we synthesize the nonlinear relationships between built environment attributes and three types of travel behavior: driving, transit, and active travel. Forty-eight studies using non- or semi-parametric models are identified, primarily conducted in China and the United States. The aggregated relationships suggest that built environment elements exhibit moderate effects on travel behavior and show nonlinear associations. We further identify common thresholds at which built environment factors simultaneously affect multiple travel behaviors. Finally, we highlight key directions for future research, including establishing causal relationships, examining spatial and contextual heterogeneity, and uncovering underlying mechanisms.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Measuring transit riders’ heat exposure and mitigation during the 2021 Vancouver heatwave
Authors: Henry Shaver, Luyu Liu, Naser Ahmed, Jed A. Long, James A. Voogt, Ehab Diab, Jinfei Wang, Jinhyung Lee
Abstract: Previous research on transit riders’ vulnerability to heat often relies on coarse approximations of thermal comfort or unintuitive measures of exposure. Moreover, despite the potential for shade and transit shelters to mitigate heat, little research has considered their availability throughout transit journeys. Using the 2021 extreme heat event in Vancouver, BC, Canada as a case study, we integrate high-resolution urban microclimate models and transit trip simulations to assess the socio-spatial patterns of risk faced by transit riders. We propose four intuitive measures that describe what residents departing from different neighbourhoods can expect in terms of potential exposure and mitigation availability, on average, when travelling anywhere across the transit network. We leverage these metrics for social equity analysis. We find that significantly larger shares of marginalized populations live in neighbourhoods with the highest exposure and lowest levels of mitigation, highlighting the urgent need for equity-focused climate adaptation policies in transit systems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Machine learning-informed uncertainty analysis in life cycle assessment of alternative marine fuels
Authors: Run Liu, Jing Wang, Ran Yan
Abstract: Life cycle assessment (LCA) evaluates the entire fuel chain environmental impacts of alternative marine fuels, yet uncertainties in input data limit its reliability. Moreover, existing LCA uncertainty analyses often fail to capture nonlinear interactions among variables and key greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions drivers. This study develops a Bayesian network (BN)-based LCA model using three container ship categories on the Singapore-Australia Green and Digital Shipping Corridor with electrolytic liquefied hydrogen (e-LH 2 ) and electro-ammonia (e-NH 3 ) as potential alternative fuels. The BN-based LCA model identifies electricity type, ship category, and sailing speed as main drivers of GHG emissions. Relative to average 2008 GHG emission levels of container ships, switching from solar- to wind-based electricity results in an additional 15% reduction for e-LH 2 and 18% for e-NH 3 , while the optimal e-LH 2 scenario achieves about 5% lower emissions than e-NH 3 . These findings provide quantitative evidence for data-driven policy advice and support IMO’s decarbonisation targets.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Smart charging of fleet and personal electric vehicles through joint vehicle-to-grid optimization
Authors: Lin Su, Navjyoth Jayashankar, Krishna Murthy Gurumurthy, Kara M. Kockelman
Abstract: As electric vehicle (EV) adoption accelerates, vehicle-to-grid (V2G) strategies offer advantages over unmanaged charging (V0G) by enhancing grid stability, reducing fleet operation costs, and supporting integration of variable generation resources. This research develops a day-ahead optimization framework linked with agent-based simulations to evaluate coordinated V2G participation by fleet and personal EVs under 5 energy-pricing settings in Austin, Texas. Three scenarios (V0G, fleet-only V2G, and joint-V2G) are examined, considering real-time price and grid profiles, health-damage costs, and operational constraints for both fleet and personal EVs. Results show how V2G scenarios shift fleet EV charging to mid-day while enabling strategic battery-discharge during evening peaks, mitigating grid stress and lowering EV energy costs. V2G delivers close to 80% energy-cost savings for a 2000-EV fleet in Austin on grid-stressed days, with 55% lower charging pollutant outputs. Joint-V2G amplifies system-level benefits by complementing fleet discharge, but smart-charging equipment costs can offset those benefits.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Electric vehicle charging management through LSTM-based prediction of non-critical charging sessions
Authors: Hanif Tayarani, Gil Tal, Christopher J. Nitta
Abstract: Battery electric vehicles (BEVs) reduce more GHG emissions when charging aligns with low-carbon electricity. Many real-world sessions happen during high-emission hours but are not necessary for completing daily travel. This study develops a deep learning model that helps drivers skip or shift these non-critical sessions to cleaner hours without changing travel routines. We train a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network using second-by-second data from 64 BEVs. The model forecasts travel needs for the next two days and identifies non-critical charging sessions. It then shifts those sessions to lower-emission hours. Results show up to 41% GHG reduction and 49% fewer charging days. A 6 kW charger performs nearly as well as a 19 kW charger without requiring costly infrastructure upgrades. Tests in CAISO, PJM, and ERCOT show consistent improvements, even in grids with less daytime renewables. This approach offers a scalable path to decarbonize transport without new infrastructure or changes to driver behavior.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Fuel efficiency in ferry services: GPS-based clustering and explainable AI
Authors: Robert Klar, Nina Svensson, Petra Stelling, Vangelis Angelakis
Abstract: Enhancing fuel efficiency in ferry operations is essential for reducing emissions and advancing maritime sustainability. This study presents a data-driven framework that uses second-level GPS data enriched with operational and environmental variables to identify and explain fuel consumption patterns. Vessel movements are segmented into trip legs and journeys, and operational metrics such as speed, wind exposure, and fuel use are computed. A hybrid machine learning approach combines unsupervised clustering to detect recurring operational patterns with gradient boosting models and explainable methods to quantify feature impacts. The framework achieves strong performance, with a cluster classification accuracy of 94 percent and a coefficient of determination of 0.97 for fuel prediction. Results indicate that operational speed is the dominant driver of fuel consumption, while analysis of captain assignments reveals the influence of human factors. The proposed framework provides actionable insights for speed management and operational optimization, enabling cost-effective emission reductions in ferry services.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Electric vehicle policy dilemma: maximizing social welfare vs minimizing cost
Authors: Abhishek Chakraborty, Sumit Sarkar, Apratim Guha
Abstract: Promoting the adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) through evolving government policies involves complex strategic interactions with stakeholders like manufacturers, consumers, and the government. Our study compares two models when the government either maximizes social welfare or minimizes costs, given an exogenous EV adoption target. Assuming a single manufacturer for EVs and gasoline vehicles (GVs), we mainly focus on government policies. We find that, regardless of type, the government prefers combining consumer subsidies and investment in charging infrastructure. We also establish that consumer subsidy, EV price, and optimal level of charging infrastructure for a social welfare-maximizing government are higher whenever the target adoption level for a cost-minimizing government is below a threshold. Further, government and private investments in charging infrastructure complement each other rather than crowding each other out. We study the robustness of our findings by considering EV drivers’ range anxiety, duopoly, and external consumer nudge.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: How the built environment characteristics shape parents’ perception of active commuting norms
Authors: Hanna Forsberg, Pablo Campos-Garzón, Ana Ruiz Alarcón, Iris Díaz- Carrasco, Sergio Campos- Sánchez, Palma Chillón, Francisco Javier Huertas-Delgado
Abstract: Active commuting to school (ACS) is a promising strategy to increase physical activity among adolescents. While characteristics of the built environment influence commuting behaviors, they may also shape parents’ perceptions of social norms related to ACS. This study analyses how subjective and objective built environment characteristics, at both micro- and macro-scale, are associated with parents’ perceptions of the social norm. When the built environment was considered as whole in a multivariable model, only the density of sports facilities (a macro-scale measure) was linked to parents’ perception of social norms, while subjective and micro-scale characteristics were not. These findings imply that environments with visible opportunities for physical activity, such as sports facilities, may shape parental perceptions of ACS as normative behavior. The presence and design of such facilities could be considered in planning, with macro-scale variables emerging as the most informative measure capturing associations with the social norm.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Environmental impact assessment for a sustainable urban freight transport system
Authors: Liangyu Chen, Ni Sheng, Yuzhen Ma, Yuanyuan Wan
Abstract: This study proposes a conceptual framework for a Sustainable Urban Freight Transport System (SUFTS) and interprets its realization primarily through three interrelated determinants: infrastructural, technological, and managerial factors. The study selects an Urban Green Freight Transport Distribution Demonstration Project (UGFT) implemented in China as a case study. The conceptual contribution lies in this framework, while the empirical contribution lies in operationalizing it through a systematic environmental impact assessment of UGFT as an integrated policy package, thereby addressing a gap where such assessments often focus on individual dimensions of green freight initiatives. Results show that the UGFT significantly improves overall urban air quality in pilot cities, but the effects weaken after the first two years. Moreover, spatial spillover benefits of the policy exist within a 200 km radius.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: From bigger batteries to new charging realities
Authors: Weipeng Zhan, Yuan Liao, Sonia Yeh, Junjun Deng, Zhenpo Wang, Dingsong Cui
Abstract: The rapid adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) with increasingly advanced battery technologies is reshaping electricity demand patterns. Yet existing studies often assume static behaviors, overlooking that real-world charging patterns are transient and evolve in response to technological change. This study applies a scenario-aware generative modeling framework to project weekly EV charging demand in Beijing for 2030, capturing behavioral shifts driven by evolving battery technologies, usage patterns, and infrastructure conditions. Results indicate that total charging load could increase by 457–509% compared to a 2021 baseline under two different scenarios of battery size growth. Though medium-power (4–20 kW) charging remains dominant in event frequency, high-power ( > 20 kW) charging contributes substantially to loads, implying the growing risk of stress on the power grid in the absence of coordinated scheduling. The proposed framework provides a scalable, data-driven method to simulate EV usage and load patterns and offers valuable insights for transportation and energy planners confronting the rapid electrification of private mobility.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Multi-criteria well-to-wheel sustainability assessment of energy pathways for China’s new energy vehicles
Authors: Shuo Zhang, Ji Feng, Hongtao Ren, Yadong Yu
Abstract: Achieving transport decarbonization requires evaluating the sustainability of upstream energy systems that support new energy vehicles (NEV). This study develops an integrated multi-criteria framework combining well-to-wheel life-cycle environmental assessment, levelized cost accounting, and stakeholder-informed weighting to compare 28 energy pathways for battery electric vehicles (BEVs), fuel cell vehicles, and internal combustion engine vehicles using synthetic e-Fuels. Results indicate that BEV pathways supplied by low-carbon electricity generally show favorable environmental and economic performance, while ICEV pathways using grid-electrolysis e-Fuels perform the worst. Among hydrogen pathways, grid-electrolysis with gaseous-hydrogen trailers has the highest well-to-pump cost (CNY 51.93 per 105 kJ), whereas coal-gasification with pipeline delivery is lowest (CNY 17.55 per 105 kJ). Although renewable hydrogen routes currently entail higher costs, they show substantial long-term potential as costs decline. These findings offer critical insights for investment priorities and infrastructure strategies to accelerate NEV adoption.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Network-scale carbon mitigation potential of truck platooning via large-scale trajectory data
Authors: Denghui Pan, Chuanzhi Thomas Xie, Aoyong Li, Shuyue Qian, Yilong Ren, Haiyang Yu
Abstract: Truck platooning is a promising strategy to reduce carbon emissions in freight transport, but its real-world mitigation potential across large-scale traffic networks has not been fully quantified. This study develops a data-driven framework to empirically evaluate the carbon reduction effects of truck platooning using eight months of high-resolution GPS trajectories. Advanced map-matching, an enhanced Longest Common Subsequence trajectory similarity method, and graph-based clustering are applied to identify spontaneous platooning events and estimate associated emission reductions. The framework also enables analysis of the spatiotemporal distribution of platooning opportunities across a regional road network. Results indicate that fully exploiting observed spontaneous platooning could cut total fuel consumption by 11.8% compared with a no-platooning baseline. Notably, only 35.8% of platoons occur within a single enterprise, highlighting the importance of cross-company coordination. These findings provide empirical evidence and methodological support for policymakers and industry stakeholders to promote sustainable freight transport through effective platooning strategies.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Facilitating sustainable urban air mobility: Social influence and human oversight
Authors: Woojae Kim, Hyeonjun Jin, Kyuho Maeng
Abstract: Urban air mobility (UAM) has emerged as a promising solution for reducing carbon emissions and enhancing urban sustainability. However, widespread consumer acceptance is critical for realizing these benefits. This study examines the relationship between technological and non-technological determinants using a discrete choice experiment with 511 respondents.
